Because it is the integral spirit of Islam to consider every Muslim free of such sin; anything contrary to that established reality, put forward without proof, is a lie, and no further proof is needed.

Ayah 17 seals it: *Allah admonishes you never to return to the like of it, if you are believers.* Ibn Kathir: Allah forbids and warns you against ever doing anything like this again in the future; "if you are believers" means if you believe in Allah and His laws and respect His Messenger ﷺ. The bar is *abadan*, forever.

## Ayah 18 and living it

The passage closes: *And Allah makes the signs clear to you, and Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.* Ibn Kathir: He makes clear to you the rulings of the Shari'ah and His divine decrees; He knows what is right for His servants and He is Wise in His laws and decrees.

**The first move is the good assumption** — ayah 12 does not ask you to be neutral, it asks you to think well and to say so aloud. **Ask for the evidence, and if it is not there, refuse to carry the news.** **What passes through the mind is pardoned; what leaves the tongue is not.**

And if you are the one wronged, ayah 11 is for you. 'A'ishah took refuge in the words of Ya'qub — patience is most fitting, and Allah's help is sought — and Allah answered with revelation recited until the end of time. Her response when vindicated is the model: I will give praise to no one except Allah, for He is the One who has proven my innocence.

passages.title: Loving indecency to spread, and the duty to pardon
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat close the discussion of the slander (*ifk*) against ʿĀʾishah by turning from the incident itself to the disease behind it: the appetite some people have for seeing filth attached to believers, and the hardness that lingers in a wronged heart even after the truth comes out. Ayah 19 passes sentence on those who *love* scandal to spread; ayat 20 and 21 twice interrupt the warning with "had it not been for Allah's grace and His mercy upon you," framing a command not to walk in Shayṭān's footsteps; and ayah 22 brings the whole thing down to one man's oath — Abū Bakr's — and asks him, and us, a question we cannot answer safely except one way.

## Ayah 19: the sin of wanting it to spread

Ibn Kathīr reads ayah 19 as **the third instance of discipline** in this sequence, aimed specifically "at those who hear evil talk, believe it to some extent, and start to spread it" — and his conclusion for them is blunt: "they should not spread such talk or pass it on to others."

Notice what the ayah actually condemns. It does not say "those who spread indecency." It says **those who *love* that indecency should spread** among the believers. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out this "extra element" precisely: those who propagate such rumours "actually want the spread of obscenity and immorality among the Muslims." The transmitter may protest that he meant no harm, that he was only sharing news. The Qurʼān looks past the excuse to the appetite underneath — the small pleasure a heart takes in a believer's disgrace. Ibn Kathīr glosses it simply as "those who like to see evil talk about them appear."

A note on the word rendered "indecency." Ibn Kathīr's translation keeps it in Arabic — *Fāḥishah* — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it "shamelessness." How Ibn Kathīr reads it *in this context* is visible in the heading he gives the section: "Disciplining Those Who Like That Illegal Sexual Intercourse Should Be Circulated Among the Believers."

**The two-fold punishment.** "For them is a painful torment in this world and the Hereafter." Ibn Kathīr specifies: in this world, *because of the prescribed punishment*, and in the Hereafter, "because of the torment in Hell." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a sobering rider: the punishment of the Hereafter follows the Day of Judgement and so cannot be experienced here, but the worldly one can be seen — and those who were punished for the false accusation have in fact already tasted it. And if someone escapes that worldly punishment because the proof required to impose it was lacking, "even then he has earned the punishment," to be carried out in the Hereafter. Escaping the court is not escaping the account.

**"And Allah knows and you know not."** Ibn Kathīr's gloss is short and freeing: *return the matter to Him and you will be guided.* When a story reaches you about a believer, you are not the one with the facts. He is. Hand it back to Him rather than filling the gap with your own guesswork.

## The system the Qurʼān built against obscenity

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān steps back here to explain the design the Qurʼān has drawn out, and it is worth following carefully. The arrangement is that, first, such news should not be spread at all; and if it does leak out, it must be backed by lawful proof, so that the punishment for adultery is carried out publicly, immediately after the news spreads. In that arrangement, **the publicity itself serves as a preventive measure** — people never hear of the crime without seeing what it costs.

Remove the condition of lawful proof and the whole mechanism inverts. It becomes easy to pass on and publicise such scandals, "especially, when there is no punishment attached to it." And, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān argues, the absence of any fear about spreading scandals wears away people's revulsion at immorality and obscenity, and even encourages indulging in such crimes and propagating them. Its everyday example is the newspaper: young men and women read such stories frequently, and as a result "the intensity of such wicked acts is minimized gradually, and instead a slow inclination for indulging in them develops in their minds." The commentary's example was the daily paper; a reader today can supply a far more relentless version without any strain. This is why the Qurʼān permits such news to circulate only where it is supported by lawful evidence — and why, where there is neither proof nor punishment, it declares the publicity of such news "a tool for spreading obscenity among the Muslims." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls this "a vital point [that] needs to be pondered by the Muslims."

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathīr records here that Imam Aḥmad reported from Thawbān that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Do not annoy the servants of Allah, nor abuse them, nor seek their hidden shortcomings. Whoever seeks out the faults of his Muslim brother, Allah will expose his faults and degrade him, even if he is hiding in his house." The punishment matches the crime exactly: the man who hunts for another's covering finds his own removed.

## Ayah 20: the sentence Allah does not finish

"And had it not been for the grace of Allah and His mercy upon you, and that Allah is full of kindness, Most Merciful…" — and then nothing. The consequence is left hanging. Ibn Kathīr supplies what the silence implies: "if it were not for this, it would have been another matter altogether." The unspoken result is more frightening than any stated one; the community is left to imagine for itself what it had just narrowly escaped.

Ibn Kathīr explains the two names in this ayah in terms of what Allah actually did in this affair: He is "full of kindness towards His servants and Merciful towards them" — **He accepts the repentance of those who repent to Him from this sin, and He purifies those among them who are purified by the prescribed punishment carried out on them.** That last phrase reframes the penalty entirely. For a believer who repents, it is not merely a debt collected; it is a cleansing.

## Ayah 21: the footsteps

Then the address changes to a direct call: **"O you who believe! Do not follow the footsteps of Shayṭān."** Ibn Kathīr: this means "his ways and paths and what he commands."

The early authorities Ibn Kathīr gathers each open a different angle on the phrase **khuṭuwāt al-Shayṭān**:

- **Ibn ʿAbbās** (recorded by ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah): his *deeds*.
- **ʿIkrimah**: his *evil whispers*.
- **Qatādah**: "Every sin is one of the footsteps of Shayṭān."
- **Abū Mijlaz**: "Vowing to commit sin is one of the footsteps of Shayṭān."

Read together, these run from the outermost act inward to the innermost stirring. And the word the ayah chooses is *footsteps* — a following taken one pace at a time. Abū Mijlaz's remark is the sharpest of the four: on his reading, the vow to commit a sin is already a step taken, before the hand or tongue has moved at all.

Then the reason for the prohibition: **"whoever follows the footsteps of Shayṭān — he commands immorality and evil deeds."** Ibn Kathīr calls this "a warning given in the most concise and eloquent manner." The logic is compressed into a single line: you do not get to choose which of his steps you take. Follow him at all and you have taken a guide whose entire instruction is immorality and evil deeds. There is nothing else down that road.

**The second "had it not been for."** The ayah then repeats the phrase with a different, and devastating, completion: "not one of you would ever have been pure from sins." Ibn Kathīr: if Allah "did not help whomever He wills to repent and come back to Him and be purified from Shirk, evil and sin, and whatever bad characteristics each person has according to his nature, no one would ever attain purity and goodness."

Read that against the whole passage. Some of the community were punished; some repented; some were spared. Nobody in the story stands on their own cleanness. **Tazkiyah** — the purification of the self that the ayah speaks of — is not something a person achieves and then owns; it is granted. "But Allah purifies whom He wills," which Ibn Kathīr explains as: among His creation — "and He sends astray whomever He wills, leaving him to be doomed in his misguidance and sin." The ayah gives no one a claim on Him.

It closes with two of Allah's names, which we affirm as He affirmed them, without likening Him to His creation and without emptying them of meaning. Ibn Kathīr takes them as fitted exactly to this context: **as-Samīʿ**, the All-Hearer — "He hears what His servants say"; and **al-ʿAlīm**, the All-Knower — "of who deserves to be guided and who deserves to be misguided." Every word said in the rumour was heard as it was spoken.

## Ayah 22: Abū Bakr and Misṭaḥ

Now the passage stops preaching and touches a nerve.

Ibn Kathīr and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān both give the background. **Misṭaḥ ibn Uthāthah** was Abū Bakr's cousin — the son of his maternal aunt — "a poor man with no wealth except whatever Abū Bakr spent on him," and one of those who had migrated for the sake of Allah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that Misṭaḥ and Ḥassān were both illustrious Companions who had taken part in the battle of Badr, but that they slipped on this occasion. Ibn Kathīr states it more starkly still: Misṭaḥ "had invented the lies and the slander." Then Allah accepted his repentance from that, and the prescribed punishment was carried out upon him. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that the Prophet ﷺ awarded them the punishment for false accusation after the ayat of exoneration came down — and that just as ʿĀʾishah's innocence was declared by Allah, so too was it declared that the repentance of these believers was accepted and they were pardoned.

Abū Bakr was, in Ibn Kathīr's words, "known for his generosity" and did favours "to his relatives and strangers alike." But this was his daughter. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes a father's love for his daughter surging up and, as a natural corollary, annoyance with Misṭaḥ, since her feelings had been deeply injured by him — and Abū Bakr swore an oath that he would never help him materially again.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes a point here that keeps the ayah honest. Helping any *specific* poor person is not obligatory for a Muslim, and stopping material help one used to give is not a sin. Abū Bakr had broken no law. **But Allah willed to make this illustrious group of Companions a model for the society.** So the same revelation that granted the ones who slipped divine help to repent sincerely and reform themselves now took the ones who had sworn off their charity out of natural grief and displeasure, and imparted to them "wisdom of supreme ethics": break the oath, expiate for it, and give. "It is below their dignity to stop the material help. They should also forgive and overlook, the way Allah has forgiven them."

**The language.** The verb **yaʾtali** means, as both Maʿārif ul Qurʼān and Ibn Kathīr note, *to swear* — to make an oath. And notice how the addressees are named. Because helping Misṭaḥ was never a religious obligation, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that the Qurʼān adopts a different line: those whom Allah has bestowed knowledge and excellence, and granted the means to spend in His way, "should be careful not to undertake such an oath" — and the words **ulū al-faḍl minkum wa-l-saʿah**, "the men of grace and wealth," are used to put that meaning across. Ibn Kathīr glosses "those among you who are blessed with graces" as those who have the means to give charity and do good, and "and wealth" as good fortune. The verse says, in effect: *you are better than this.*

The three named recipients — kinsmen, the poor, and those who left their homes for Allah's cause — all describe Misṭaḥ at once. Ibn Kathīr: do not swear that you will not uphold the ties of kinship with relatives who are needy or who migrated for the sake of Allah, "which is the ultimate act of kindness in the area of upholding kinship ties."

**"Let them pardon and forgive"** — Ibn Kathīr: past insults and bad treatment. And then he lifts the eye upward: this instruction is itself "part of the patience, generosity and kindness of Allah towards His creation, despite the fact that they wrong themselves." He is teaching them to deal with each other the way He deals with all of them.

## The question that ends the argument

**"Do you not love that Allah should forgive you?"**

Ibn Kathīr says this "shows that the reward fits the action, and that *if you forgive others, you will be forgiven*." The ayah does not order Abū Bakr to feel differently. It asks him what he wants from Allah — and lets him see that the hand he is closing is the same hand he is holding out.

He answered at once. Ibn Kathīr records his words: **"Of course, by Allah, we love — O our Lord — that You should forgive us."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the same moment, saying that Abū Bakr replied immediately that he certainly wants Allah to forgive him, and citing Bukhārī and Muslim for it. Then, in Ibn Kathīr's account, he resumed his spending on Misṭaḥ and said, "By Allah I will never stop spending on him" — deliberately counteracting what he had said before, "By Allah I will never spend on him." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the same reversal: he restored the help and said it would never stop now. Ibn Kathīr's verdict on the moment: "This proves that he deserved to be called aṣ-Ṣiddīq, may Allah be pleased with him and his daughter."

That is the measure of the man. The gap between the oath and its reversal was one question long.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān closes by relaying, from the Ṣaḥīḥ of Bukhārī on the authority of ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar, that the Prophet ﷺ said: he is not the one truly kind-hearted towards relatives who merely returns their favours; the one truly kind-hearted towards relatives is he who maintains the relationship with them even after they have severed it. (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān marks this report as coming through the tafsir Mazharī, so it reaches us here at one remove rather than quoted directly from the Ṣaḥīḥ.) Misṭaḥ had cut the tie in the cruellest way imaginable. Abū Bakr joined it back.

## Living it

- **Check the appetite, not just the act.** Ayah 19 condemns *loving* that indecency should spread among the believers. Before forwarding, ask honestly whether some part of you enjoys the story.
- **Refuse to be a link in the chain.** Ibn Kathīr's "third discipline" is aimed at those who hear evil talk, half-believe it, and pass it on. Not originating a rumour is no defence.
- **Where there is no proof, there is no news** — only, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, "a tool for spreading obscenity among the Muslims."
- **Do not go hunting.** "Whoever seeks out the faults of his Muslim brother, Allah will expose his faults" — recorded by Imam Aḥmad from Thawbān.
- **Watch the small steps.** Qatādah: every sin is one of Shayṭān's footsteps. Abū Mijlaz: even the vow to commit one is.
- **Do not let anger cost you a tie you are meant to carry.** When withdrawing generosity breaks no law but is beneath you, ayah 22 says: be greater than your grievance.
- **Answer the question.** Do you not love that Allah should forgive you? Then say what Abū Bakr said — and then do what he did.

passages.title: The curse on accusers and the Day limbs testify
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat close the account of the slander against Sayyidah ʿĀʾishah bint aṣ-Ṣiddīq, may Allah be pleased with them both. Having already legislated the punishment for false accusation earlier in the sūrah, Allah now turns from the courtroom to the conscience: ayah 23 pronounces a curse in both worlds on those who slandered and never took it back; ayah 24 shows the Day their own bodies will testify against them; ayah 25 shows the recompense paid out in full and Allah known at last as *al-Ḥaqq al-Mubīn*, the Manifest Truth; and ayah 26 lifts the whole matter onto a principle — the pure belong with the pure — which is at once ʿĀʾishah's vindication and a mirror held up to her accusers.

What holds the four together is a single movement: **the tongue that spoke the lie in this world is silenced in the next, and the truth is spoken instead — by the liar's own limbs.**

## Why a second, harsher warning?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the obvious question. Ayah 4 has already legislated eighty lashes and permanent rejection of the accuser's testimony; ayah 5 then opens a door — *"except those who repent afterwards and mend their ways; then, Allah is All-Forgiving, Very-Merciful."* So is ayah 23 simply a repetition?

No, and the difference is precisely the missing exception. Ayah 5 exempts the repentant. Ayah 23 announces a curse in this world and the Hereafter **with no exception at all**.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing *Bayān al-Qurʼān*) draws the conclusion: this ayah is aimed at those who were involved in slandering Sayyidah ʿĀʾishah and *did not repent* — who clung to the accusation and kept propagating it even after her exoneration was revealed in the Qurʼān. No Muslim could do such a thing; whoever disregards a categorical Qurʼānic injunction cannot remain a Muslim. So the ones addressed here are the hypocrites who never stopped their campaign against her.

The two groups are thus sorted by two different endings. Those who felt remorse were given the glad tiding of deliverance from punishment in *"Allah is All-Forgiving, Very-Merciful"* (ayah 5). Those who did not were warned in *"On the Day their tongues, their hands and their legs will testify against them"* (ayah 24).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a sober note on the aftermath: the few Muslims who got involved in the episode did so **before** the verses of her exoneration were revealed. After that revelation, whoever makes an insinuation against her character is a disbeliever and a denier of the Qurʼān — and it names a few Shīʿī groups and some other individuals who are involved in that practice as falling under this, regarded as disbelievers by the consensus of the entire Ummah.

Ibn Kathīr states the ruling in the same terms: all of the scholars agree that whoever slanders her or makes accusations against her *after what has been said in this ayah* is a disbeliever, because of his being obstinate with the Qurʼān — and the same ruling applies to all of the Mothers of the Believers.

## The three words of ayah 23

The women protected in ayah 23 are described by three qualities stacked one on the next:

- **al-muḥṣanāt** — the chaste women.
- **al-ghāfilāt** — rendered "unsuspecting," and by Maʿārif ul Qurʼān "naive"; Ibn Kathīr's fuller gloss is those *"who never even think of anything touching their chastity."*
- **al-muʾmināt** — the believing women. Ibn Kathīr ties the third quality to the second: such a woman never even thinks of anything affecting her chastity *since* she is a good believer.

Ibn Kathīr then sets the scope. This is a warning and a threat from Allah to those who accuse such women — and **the Mothers of the Believers are more entitled to be included in this category than any other chaste woman**, especially the one who was the reason for this ayah being revealed: ʿĀʾishah bint aṣ-Ṣiddīq.

That the curse falls **"in this life and in the Hereafter"** places the accusers, as Ibn Kathīr notes, alongside another ayah: *"Verily, those who annoy Allah and His Messenger"* (33:57).

And the ayah's reach does not stop in the seventh century. ʿAbd ar-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said: *"This is about ʿĀʾishah, and whoever does anything similar nowadays to Muslim women, the same applies to him, but ʿĀʾishah is the one who is primarily referred to here."* The occasion of revelation is specific; the warning is live.

## Among the seven destroyers

The gravity of this sin is not left to inference. Ibn Kathīr records, through Ibn Abī Ḥātim, that Abū Hurayrah said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: **"Shun the seven destructive sins."** He was asked what they were, and he ﷺ answered: associating partners with Allah; magic; killing a soul whom Allah has forbidden to be killed, except with just cause; consuming *ribā*; consuming the property of orphans; desertion at the time of war; and **accusing chaste women, who never even think of anything touching their chastity and are good believers**. Ibn Kathīr notes that this was recorded by al-Bukhārī and Muslim in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs.

Notice that the last item is given in the Prophet's ﷺ words with the very phrasing of ayah 23. Slander of a chaste woman stands on a list beside shirk, murder, and desertion at the time of war — sins named as destructive to the one who commits them.

## Ayah 24: the Day the limbs speak

*"On the Day their tongues, their hands and their legs will testify against them of what they used to do."*

**Why would anyone need such witnesses?** Ibn Kathīr records, through Ibn Abī Ḥātim, that Ibn ʿAbbās said this refers to the idolaters, who — when they realise that no one will enter Paradise except the people who used to perform Ṣalāh — will say, *"Come, let us deny everything."* So they will deny everything; then their mouths will be sealed and their hands and feet will testify against them, and they will not be able to hide anything from Allah. The testimony of the limbs is Allah's answer to the reflex of denial.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes the same scene from the other side, noting that it is related in aḥādīth that on that Day those who **admit** their sins will be pardoned by Allah, and He will conceal their sins from the crowd of people. It is the one who denies his sins — who claims he did not commit them, and says the angels did not write his record correctly — whose speech is taken away from him, so that his hands and feet are asked to testify instead. Admission before Allah is met with pardon and concealment; denial is what makes the body speak.

**The Prophet's ﷺ smile.** Ibn Kathīr records, again through Ibn Abī Ḥātim, that Anas ibn Mālik said: we were with the Prophet ﷺ and he smiled so broadly that his back teeth could be seen, then he said, *"Do you know why I am smiling?"* We said, "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: *because of the way a person will dispute with his Lord.* He will say, "O Lord, did You not protect me from doing wrong?" Allah will say, "Of course." The person will say, "I will not accept for anyone to give testimony concerning me except myself." Allah will say, "You are sufficient as a witness against yourself." Then a seal will be put upon his mouth, and it will be said to his faculties, *"Speak"* — so they will speak about his deeds. Then he will be permitted to speak, and he will say: **"Away with you! I was only speaking in your defence!"** Ibn Kathīr notes this was recorded by Muslim and an-Nasāʾī.

The man demands that no one testify against him but himself — and Allah grants exactly that. His own body is himself. He wanted a trial with no external witness; he gets one, and loses.

**A question of apparent conflict.** Ayah 24 says their *tongues* will testify, while 36:65 says *"Today We set a seal on their mouths."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers that there is no contradiction between the two verses: the point of both is that they will not be able to use their tongues at their discretion as they do in this world. Their tongues will say only the right things, against their intent and wish. It is also possible that at a certain time their mouths and tongues will be completely sealed, and then the tongues are commanded to speak the truth — and only Allah knows best. Either way, the faculty that once served the lie is taken out of the liar's hands.

## Ayah 25: paid in full, and Allah known as He is

*"On that Day, Allah will give them their just penalty in full."* Ibn Kathīr's rendering runs: *"On that Day Allah will pay them the recompense of their deeds in full, and they will know that Allah, He is the Manifest Truth."*

On the word **dīnahum**: Ibn ʿAbbās said it means *"their account"* — and he added that every time *dīnahum* appears in the Qurʼān it means "their account." Ibn Kathīr notes this was also the view of other scholars. The recompense is not partial: it is paid **in full**.

And what dawns on them at that moment: *"they will know that Allah, He is the Manifest Truth."* Ibn Kathīr explains this to mean that His promise, His threat and His reckoning are all just, and there is no unfairness in them. In this world the accusers gambled that the truth could be bent by repetition. On that Day the Truth is no longer something argued over; it is simply known.

## Ayah 26: like belongs with like

*"Vile women are for vile men, and vile men are for vile women. And good women are for good men and good men are for good women. Those are free from what they (the accusers) say. For them there is forgiveness and a graceful provision."*

The commentators give two readings of *al-khabīthāt* / *aṭ-ṭayyibāt*, and both are reported in the sources.

**First reading: words.** Ibn ʿAbbās said: *"Evil words are for evil men, and evil men are for evil words; good words are for good men and good men are for good words. This was revealed concerning ʿĀʾishah and the people of the slander."* Ibn Kathīr notes that the same was narrated from Mujāhid, ʿAṭāʾ, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, ash-Shaʿbī, al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Ḥabīb ibn Abī Thābit and aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, and that it was the view favoured by Ibn Jarīr, who interpreted it to mean that evil speech is more suited to evil people and good speech to good people. What the hypocrites attributed to ʿĀʾishah was more suited to them, while she was most suited to innocence and to having nothing to do with them.

**Second reading: people.** ʿAbd ar-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam read it of persons: *"Evil women are for evil men and evil men are for evil women, and good women are for good men and good men are for good women."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān develops this second sense as a general principle: Allah has created a connection between people of the same nature. The vulgar and unchaste incline toward the vulgar and unchaste; the pure and chaste incline toward the pure and decent. So everyone seeks a spouse according to his or her own inclination, and in a natural way does find one to suit.

**Where the argument lands.** Both readings arrive at the same conclusion, and Ibn Kathīr states it plainly: Allah would not have made ʿĀʾishah the wife of His Messenger ﷺ unless she had been good, because he ﷺ is the best of the best of mankind. Had she been evil, she would not have been a suitable partner — neither according to Allah's Laws nor His decree. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it the same way: the messengers, who are models of purity and chastity outwardly and inwardly, are granted spouses in accordance with their status; and the Prophet ﷺ, the head of all messengers, was bestowed with spouses befitting his position in purity, chastity and ethical excellence — Sayyidah ʿĀʾishah the most prominent among them all. Only those who have no faith in the Prophet ﷺ himself can have any doubt or suspicion about her.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān anticipates an objection. The Qurʼān mentions that the wives of Sayyidnā Nūḥ and Sayyidnā Lūṭ (peace be upon them) were disbelievers — so can a prophet's wife not be bad? The answer distinguishes two different things: it is also established that those two women were not involved in any obscenity or vulgarity. Sayyidnā Ibn ʿAbbās said, *"Never did any wife of a messenger commit adultery"* (as cited in *ad-Durr al-Manthūr*). It is therefore corroborated that a messenger's wife could be a disbeliever, but could not be vulgar and sexually immoral — because adultery is a naturally detestable act in the eyes of people, whereas disbelief is not detestable in that natural way. The objection therefore does not touch the argument of ayah 26.

**"Those are free from what they say."** Ibn Kathīr: they are remote from what the people of slander and enmity say. Then two gifts follow. *"For them there is forgiveness"* — Ibn Kathīr explains this comes to them because of the lies that were told about them. And *"a graceful provision"* — meaning, with Allah in the Gardens of Delight; which, he notes, implies a promise that she will be the wife of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in Paradise. The slander meant to strip her of honour ends by securing her honour forever.

## Living it

**Guard the tongue as an organ that will one day testify.** The most sobering image in the passage is a man arguing his innocence and then rounding on his own limbs — *"Away with you! I was only speaking in your defence!"* The faculties that did the deed are the witnesses that speak about it.

**Admit, do not deny.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's contrast is practical: the one who admits his sin on that Day is pardoned and has it concealed from the crowd; the one who denies it is the one whose hands and feet are made to testify. Repentance now is infinitely cheaper than argument then.

**Take the reach of ayah 23 personally.** By ʿAbd ar-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam's reading, whoever does to a Muslim woman today anything similar to what was done to ʿĀʾishah falls under the same warning — and the Prophet ﷺ listed accusing chaste believing women among the seven destructive sins. That includes the forwarded rumour and the repeated insinuation, not only the invented one.

**Let ayah 26 govern your own character before you use it to judge others.** The principle that like belongs with like is first of all a question to ask oneself: what kind of speech do I find myself at home in? Evil speech is more suited to evil people. The safest way to be free of a slander is to be the sort of person to whom it will never stick.

passages.title: Seeking permission before entering houses
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat teach believers how to approach another person's home: do not walk in until you have made yourself known and greeted those inside; if no one answers, do not enter; if you are turned away, turn back without resentment; public places are a different case. One principle holds them together — a home is a private space, and its door is a boundary that only permission may open.

## Where this comes in the surah

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān places this passage inside the design of Sūrah an-Nūr. The surah works to curb obscenity: it prescribes punishments, condemns those who fling false accusations at chaste people, then turns to measures that stop such things taking root at all. The rules of *istiʾdhān* — seeking permission before entering someone's house — belong to that preventive layer; their wisdom, says Maʿārif ul Qurʾān, is that a person's eye should not fall on women who are not his *maḥram* (relatives one may never marry).

The Qurʾān calls the home a blessing because it is meant to be a place of rest — *He made for you, from your houses, a place of rest* (16:80). A person can only find that rest if he can live without others intruding, so the first purpose of *istiʾdhān* is to spare people interference. The second is for the visitor's own sake: come in after asking and the host receives you with respect and attends to your need; walk in unannounced and the host wants only to be rid of you. The third is the removal of temptation — entering unannounced, one may see the women of the household. The fourth is privacy: what someone does in the solitude of his home he may not wish others to know, and exposing it is both a sin and a source of distress.

## What was being replaced

Muqātil bin Ḥayyān describes social life before this revelation. In the Jāhiliyyah, when a man met his friend he would not greet him with *salām*; he would say *Ḥuyyīta ṣabāḥan* or *Ḥuyyīta masāʾan* — "good morning," "good evening." And they did not ask permission to enter one another's houses at all: a man might walk straight in and announce, "I have come in." Muqātil adds that this was hard on a man to bear, since he might be with his wife. So Allah changed all of it by enjoining covering and chastity, making social life pure and free of sin or impropriety. Ibn Kathīr comments simply: "What Muqātil said is good."

## The word the ayah chooses: *tastaʾnisū*

Ayah 27 says: do not enter houses other than your own **ḥattā tastaʾnisū wa tusallimū ʿalā ahlihā** — until you have sought familiarity and greeted their people.

The plain word for the act commanded is *istiʾdhān*, seeking permission — and that is how the majority of commentators read the verse. But the Qurʾān uses *tastaʾnisū*, whose literal sense, Maʿārif ul Qurʾān explains, is *to seek acquaintance*: in asking, the host becomes acquainted with the visitor through his voice, so the element of surprise is removed. Ibn Kathīr records the same understanding from the early generation: al-ʿAwfī narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās that "putting people at ease means seeking permission to enter."

## How it is actually done

**Salām first, then your name.** Commentators differ over the order of the two acts in ayah 27. Qurṭubī holds one seeks permission first, and gives salām on entering once it is granted. But the way that appears *masnūn* — established by the Prophet's ﷺ practice in the narrations, says Maʿārif ul Qurʾān — is to give salām from outside and then ask to come in, naming oneself; on entering, the greeting is repeated in the usual way. Imām Bukhārī records in *al-Adab al-Mufrad* from Abū Hurayrah that if someone asks permission before greeting, the host need not answer him; Bayhaqī records in *Shuʿab al-Īmān* from Jābir that the Prophet ﷺ said, "Do not let in the one who does not greet before seeking permission."

Imām Aḥmad recorded from Kaladah bin al-Ḥanbal that at the Conquest of Makkah, Ṣafwān bin Umayyah sent him to the Prophet ﷺ with milk, a small gazelle and small cucumbers. "I entered upon the Prophet ﷺ and I did not give the greeting of *salām* nor ask for permission to enter." The Prophet ﷺ said: "Go back and say: *As-salāmu ʿalaykum, may I enter?*" This was also recorded by Abū Dāwūd, at-Tirmidhī and an-Nasāʾī; at-Tirmidhī said, "*Ḥasan Gharīb*."

**Never answer "It's me."** The Group recorded that Jābir said: "I came to the Prophet ﷺ about a debt owed by my father and knocked at the door. He said, *Who is that?* I said, 'I am!' He said, *I? I?* — as if he disliked it." Ibn Kathīr explains why: the word tells you nothing unless a man clearly states his name or the name he is known by; otherwise everyone can call himself "Me."

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān adds a failure common today: knocking, then staying silent when the household asks who is there — leaving the host in suspense, the very opposite of *uns*. By contrast, Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim records Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī asking permission of ʿUmar with, "This is Abū Mūsā — peace be upon you — this is al-Ashʿarī": first his name, then a further clarification. ʿUmar himself, Maʿārif ul Qurʾān notes, would announce at the Prophet's ﷺ door: peace be upon the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon you — may ʿUmar come in?

Knocking is itself a valid way of seeking permission, provided you give your name at the same time; and it should be gentle, not so loud as to startle the household. Those who knocked at the Prophet's ﷺ door, Maʿārif ul Qurʾān relates, used their fingernails, so the sound would not disturb him.

**Stand to the side of the door, and never peer in.** Abū Dāwūd alone recorded from ʿAbdullāh bin Busr that when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came to a door he never stood directly in front of it, but to the right or left, saying, "As-salāmu ʿalaykum, as-salāmu ʿalaykum." Ibn Kathīr notes the reason: doorways then had no covers or curtains — and Maʿārif ul Qurʾān adds that where curtains existed the wind might lift them. Peering in while you wait defeats the point; Maʿārif ul Qurʾān notes it is strongly prohibited in the ḥadīth, citing Bukhārī and Muslim from Sahl bin Saʿd as-Sāʿidī. In the Two Ṣaḥīḥs it is recorded that the Prophet ﷺ said: "If a person looks into your house without your permission, and you throw a stone at him and it puts his eye out, there will be no blame on you."

## Ayah 28: no answer, or "go back"

Ayah 28 covers two further situations. First: "if you find no one therein, still enter not until permission has been given." Ibn Kathīr reads this as the law of other people's property: the owner grants or withholds as he wishes, and an empty house does not become open ground.

Second: "And if you are asked to go back, go back — it is purer for you." Ibn Kathīr says this applies whether you are turned away before or after permission has been given. Saʿīd bin Jubayr summarised it in a phrase: "This means, do not stand at people's doors."

**Three times.** Ibn Kathīr states the settled practice: one seeks permission three times; if it is granted he may enter, otherwise he goes away. It was reported in the Ṣaḥīḥ, he says, that Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī asked ʿUmar three times, received no permission, and left. ʿUmar then said, "Did I not hear the voice of ʿAbdullāh bin Qays asking for permission? Let him come in" — but when they looked, he had gone. Asked later why he left, he said: "I asked three times and was not given permission, and I heard the Prophet ﷺ say, *If any one of you asks for permission three times and it is not given, then let him go away.*" (Maʿārif ul Qurʾān quotes the Prophet's ﷺ words themselves from Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī, citing Ibn Kathīr quoting Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī.)

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān explains the logic of three: by then the household has clearly heard, and either they cannot answer — praying, bathing, otherwise occupied — or would rather not receive a visitor now. Either way, lingering or knocking on only pressures the host.

**The Prophet ﷺ himself did it.** Ibn Kathīr transmits a narration recorded by Imām Aḥmad — from Anas or someone else, as Ibn Kathīr carefully puts it; Maʿārif ul Qurʾān reports it from Musnad Aḥmad on the authority of Anas — that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sought permission to enter upon Saʿd bin ʿUbādah, saying, "As-salāmu ʿalayka wa raḥmatullāh." Saʿd returned the greeting — but so softly that the Prophet ﷺ could not hear him. This happened three times, and then the Prophet ﷺ turned and left. Saʿd followed after him: "O Messenger of Allah, may my father and mother be ransomed for you! You did not give any greeting but I answered you — I simply did not let you hear me. I wanted to get more of your *salām* and your blessings." Saʿd acted out of overwhelming love, says Maʿārif ul Qurʾān. Even the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, at his own companion's door, turned back after three, and staying on to wait is against his sunnah, since it forces the host out.

**Turning back is *azkā*.** The ayah says going back is *azkā* — purer, cleaner for you. Qatādah relates that one of the Emigrants said: "All my life I tried to act on this ayah, but if I asked permission to visit one of my brothers and he asked me to go back, I could not do so happily" — though Allah says, *go back, it is purer for you, and Allah is All-Knower of what you do*. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān records people of past ages saying the opposite — that they spent a lifetime wishing to be turned away just once, to earn the reward of obeying this injunction, and never received that blessing.

**The host has duties too.** The visitor must accept refusal graciously. But the host is bound in turn by the Prophet's ﷺ words, "Surely your visitor has a right upon you" — to call him in, honour him, listen to him, and not refuse him without a serious excuse or genuine reason.

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān adds a related point: if someone sends a messenger to call you and you come back with that messenger, you need not seek permission. The Prophet ﷺ said, "If someone is called and he comes along with the messenger, then this by itself is permission for going in" (Abū Dāwūd, via Mazharī). But if you come later, separately, then permission must be sought as usual.

## Even those closest to you

Ibn ʿAbbās listed this among three ayat whose rulings people have abandoned: they say the most honourable is the one with the biggest house, though Allah said *the most honourable of you with Allah is the one with the most taqwā* (49:13) — "and as for seeking permission, the people have forgotten all about it." ʿAṭāʾ bin Abī Rabāḥ then asked him, "Should I seek permission to enter upon my orphan sisters who live with me in one house?" He said, "Yes." ʿAṭāʾ asked for an allowance and was refused: "Do you want to see them naked?" He pressed again, and Ibn ʿAbbās answered only, "Do you want to obey Allah? Then ask for permission."

Ibn Masʿūd said, "You must seek permission to enter upon your mothers," and Ṭāwūs said there were no women he would hate to see uncovered more than his own *maḥrams*. Imām Mālik narrates in the *Muwaṭṭaʾ* from ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasār that a man asked the Prophet ﷺ whether to seek permission before going in to his mother. He said yes — and when the man objected that he lived in the same house, and then that he was always at her service, the Prophet ﷺ each time said he must still ask: "Would you like to see your mother naked?" She may, after all, have uncovered part of herself in the house for some need.

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān draws the ruling out generally: the obligation applies to all — man or woman, *maḥram* or not. The command is grammatically addressed to men — *yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū* uses a masculine relative pronoun — but women are included, as in most Qurʾānic commands. The wives of the Companions understood themselves to be addressed: Umm Iyās said that four of them used to visit ʿĀʾishah together and would seek permission before going in. And from the ḥadīth about the mother, Maʿārif ul Qurʾān draws the meaning of *ghayra buyūtikum* in ayah 27, "other than your own houses": the house where permission is not required is the one you live in alone, with no parents, brothers or sisters residing there with you.

Even alone with one's wife there is an adab. Ibn Jurayj asked ʿAṭāʾ whether a man must seek permission to come in upon his wife; he said no — Ibn Kathīr explains this to mean not obligatory but preferable: better to let her know he is coming so as not to startle her, since she may be in a state she does not want him to see. Ibn Jarīr narrated from the nephew of Zaynab, the wife of ʿAbdullāh bin Masʿūd, that when ʿAbdullāh returned from an errand and reached the door he would clear his throat, so as not to come upon them suddenly in a state he would dislike. Ibn Kathīr says its chain of narration is Ṣaḥīḥ.

## Ayah 29: the places that are nobody's home

Ayah 29 lifts the restriction for a whole class of buildings: "There is no sin on you that you enter uninhabited houses in which you have *matāʿ*" — rightful benefit.

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān preserves the occasion of this verse. When the verses of *istiʾdhān* came down, Abū Bakr asked, "O Messenger of Allah, what will the traders of Quraysh do after this prohibition? They travel with caravans from Makkah and Madīnah to Syria, and have resting places all along the route with no permanent residents. From whom will they seek permission?" In answer, this verse was revealed (Mazharī, on the authority of Ibn Abī Ḥātim).

That occasion tells you what "uninhabited houses" means: not abandoned buildings, but places not designated for the residence of any individual or community — open to all to enter, stay in, and use. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān lists public inns, mosques, shrines, schools, hospitals, railway stations, airports: everything built for the common welfare.

*Matāʿ* means to use or benefit from something; Maʿārif ul Qurʾān takes it here in that literal sense, so the licence is tied to having genuine reason to be there. Ibn Kathīr says this ayah is *more specific* than the one before it: entering a house where nobody is present is permitted when one has a reason for doing so, such as a house prepared for guests, and where permission has been given once, that suffices. Ibn ʿAbbās expressed the relation differently, saying the general prohibition of ayah 27 was abrogated and an exception made by ayah 29 — a view also narrated from ʿIkrimah and al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī.

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān adds three limits. Conditions set by owners or organisers bind religiously too — if entering a railway platform requires a ticket, entering without one is not permissible in the Sharīʿah. Rooms reserved within such places for particular people do not count as "uninhabited houses," and entering them without permission is prohibited. And in an emergency such as a fire or a building collapsing one may enter without permission, and indeed it is desirable to go in at once.

## "And Allah knows what you do"

Ayah 28 ends, *And Allah is All-Knower of what you do*; ayah 29 ends, *And Allah has knowledge of what you reveal and what you conceal.* These are commands almost impossible to police: nobody sees the glance through a half-open door, nobody but you knows whether you walked away sincerely or nursing a grievance. So the passage grounds itself in the knowledge of Allah. Ayah 27 had already said *dhālikum khayrun lakum*, "that is better for you," which Ibn Kathīr explains as better for *both* parties, the one asking and the people inside — and *laʿallakum tadhakkarūn*, "so that you may remember."

## Living it

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān is blunt: this was the very first Islamic injunction Muslims let slip, and today even pious, educated people do not regard neglecting it as a sin or make any effort to act on it — though Ibn ʿAbbās termed even the slightest laxity or alteration in *istiʾdhān* a rejection of the Qurʾān itself.

- **Announce yourself; don't just arrive.** Maʿārif ul Qurʾān accepts modern forms: pressing a doorbell fulfils the obligation provided you then say your name audibly, and any customary local method is acceptable.
- **Apply it inside your own family.** Rooms of parents, siblings, grown children — knock.
- **Extend it to whatever a "door" is now.** Maʿārif ul Qurʾān applies the same principle to the telephone: do not call at someone's rest or prayer time unless truly urgent; before a long discussion, check they have time to talk at length. Equally, do not let a call ring unanswered — that too, it says, is against Islamic ethics, since the Prophet's ﷺ words about the visitor's right apply to the caller.

One last distinction: Maʿārif ul Qurʾān separates standing at a door *after* asking three times, which troubles the host, from waiting quietly outside without asking at all, hoping to meet someone when he emerges at his own convenience — not blameworthy, but a mark of respect. The Qurʾān itself points this way: *And if they had patience until you come out to them, that would be better for them* (49:5). Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī records Ibn ʿAbbās saying he would sometimes wait a whole afternoon at an Anṣārī companion's door to ask him about some aḥādīth rather than seek permission: "Had I sought permission he would certainly have allowed me, but I regarded that as against good manners."

The fruit of this passage is not that a man gets let in at the door, but that he becomes someone whose arrival never costs anyone their peace.

passages.title: Lowering the gaze and guarding modesty
passages.tafsir:
Ayah 30 addresses the believing men, ayah 31 the believing women, and both begin at the same place — the eye — before moving outward to the body, to dress, to who may see whom, and even to how a person walks down a street. One idea holds them together: chastity is not defended at the door of sin, but at the first glance. And because desire is a hidden thing, the passage ends not with a punishment but with a call to repentance.

## When these ayat came down

The first Qurʾanic verses on hijab, Maʿārif ul Qurʾān notes, came in Sūrah al-Aḥzāb at the time of the Prophet's ﷺ marriage to Sayyidah Zainab bint Jaḥsh (may Allah be pleased with her). The verses of Sūrah an-Nūr came later, at the time of the incident of *Ifk* — the slander against Sayyidah ʿĀʾishah — on the return from the battle of Banī al-Muṣṭaliq, in the sixth year after Hijrah.

Ibn Kathīr's comment on the command is that it is Allah's protective jealousy on behalf of the wives of His believing servants, and that it marks the believing women off from the women of Jāhiliyyah.

## Ayah 30: the command to the men

**"Lower their gaze."** The verb *yaghuḍḍu* is from the root *ghaḍḍ*, which Rāghib defines as *to bring down, to lower*. Ibn Kathīr explains it in practice: turn the eyes from what the Sharīʿah has forbidden, and if the gaze falls on something forbidden unintentionally, look away at once. Ibn Ḥibbān, cited in Maʿārif ul Qurʾān, distinguishes two cases: looking at a non-mahram woman with the intent of pleasure is totally forbidden; looking without such a motive is *makrūh* (undesirable). The ruling covers looking at anyone's private parts, man or woman, except in dire necessity such as medical examination — and it covers peeping into someone's house.

**"And guard their private parts."** Ibn Kathīr notes two senses: keeping oneself from *zinā* — unlawful sexual intercourse — as in "And those who guard their chastity" (23:5); and keeping oneself covered, as in the hadith in Musnad Aḥmad and the Sunan collections, "Guard your private parts except from your wife and those whom your right hands possess."

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān explains the ayah's structure: every possible way of satisfying unlawful desire is being shut off. The first act in that chain is a glance cast with a bad motive; its ultimate end is adultery. The Qurʾān names these two ends explicitly, and everything in between — a touch of the hands, a conversation opened for that purpose — is included by implication. Ibn Kathīr relates from Sayyidnā ʿUbaidah that any act done in disobedience to Allah is a major sin.

**"That is purer for them. Surely Allah is All-Aware of what they do."** Ibn Kathīr: purer for their hearts and better for their commitment to religion — as it has been said, whoever protects his gaze, Allah will illuminate his understanding, or his heart. Ibn Kathīr connects the closing name *Khabīr*, All-Aware, to the ayah, "Allah knows the fraud of the eyes and all that the breasts conceal" (40:19).

## From the Sunnah: the eye that is already guilty

- **The sudden glance.** Muslim recorded in his Ṣaḥīḥ that Jarīr bin ʿAbdullāh al-Bajalī (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "I asked the Prophet ﷺ about the sudden glance, and he commanded me to turn my gaze away." Maʿārif ul Qurʾān adds Sayyidnā ʿAlī's statement that the first sight is forgivable but casting the eye a second time is a sin: an unintended glance is pardoned; a deliberate glance is forbidden even the first time.
- **The rights of the road.** In the Ṣaḥīḥ, from Abū Saʿīd, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "Beware of sitting in the streets." They said, "O Messenger of Allah, we have no alternative but to sit in the streets to converse with one another." He ﷺ said, "If you insist, then give the street its rights." They asked what those rights were. He said, "Lower your gaze, return the greeting of Salam, enjoin what is good and forbid what is evil."
- **The zinā of the limbs.** In the Ṣaḥīḥ, from Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him): "The son of Adam has his share of Zina decreed for him, and he will commit that which has been decreed. The Zina of the eyes is looking; the Zina of the tongue is speaking; the Zina of the ears is listening; the Zina of the hands is striking; and the Zina of the feet is walking. The soul wishes and desires, and the private parts confirm or deny that."
- **The poisoned arrow.** Maʿārif ul Qurʾān reports, from Ṭabarānī quoting Sayyidnā ʿAbdullāh Ibn Masʿūd and citing Ibn Kathīr, that the Prophet ﷺ once said: "Casting eye is a poisonous arrow among the arrows of Satan. Whoever turns away his eye fearing from Me (despite demand of the heart), I will give him such strong faith, the delight of which he will feel in his heart."

Ibn Kathīr adds that many of the Salaf used to forbid men from staring at beardless handsome boys — presumably where one looks with bad intention and passionate desire, and Allah knows best.

## Ayah 31: the same command, then more

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān points out that women were already included in the general injunction given to men; they are then addressed separately for added emphasis.

**Do women lower the gaze in the same way?** Many held it absolutely forbidden for a woman to look at non-mahram men, whether with desire or without, citing the hadith of Sayyidah Umm Salamah: she and Maimūnah were with the Prophet ﷺ when ʿAbdullāh Ibn Umm Maktūm, the blind Companion, came in, and he ﷺ asked them to go inside. This was after the injunction of hijab had been revealed. Umm Salamah pleaded, "O Prophet of Allah, but he is only blind, he can't see us." He ﷺ replied, "Is it that you are blind too?" (Abū Dāwūd and Tirmidhī; Tirmidhī declared it *ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ*.) Other jurists held there is no harm in a woman looking at strange men without passion, citing the report in the Ṣaḥīḥ from Sayyidah ʿĀʾishah: on an ʿĪd day the Ethiopians were playing with spears in the Masjid, and the Prophet ﷺ watched while ʿĀʾishah watched from behind him, until she got bored and went away — and he did not object. Scholars are unanimous, Maʿārif ul Qurʾān concludes, that looking with lust is prohibited, and that looking without lust is still not a preferred act.

On "and protect their private parts," Ibn Kathīr transmits two readings: Saʿīd bin Jubayr said it means from immoral actions; Abū al-ʿĀliyah said every ayah of the Qurʾān that mentions guarding the private parts means guarding them from *zinā* **except** this one, which means guarding them from being seen by anybody. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān draws out the corollary that a woman may not look at another woman's *satr* — the parts that must be concealed — without lawful reason; the definition it works with is navel to knees for a man, and for a woman the whole body except face and palms.

## "Not to display their adornment except what appears of it"

*Zīnah* literally means that with which a woman adorns herself to appear attractive — fine clothes or ornaments. Since the scholars agree that clothes and ornaments not being worn, merely displayed in a market, may be looked at, the majority take *zīnah* here to mean the parts of the body on which those ornaments are worn.

Then comes the exception — "except what appears of it." **Sayyidnā ʿAbdullāh Ibn Masʿūd** explained it as the outer covering, the veil or sheet thrown over the ordinary garments, which cannot be hidden when a woman goes out on some work; on this reading it is not permitted even to uncover the face and palms before non-mahram men. Ibn Kathīr notes that al-Ḥasan, Ibn Sīrīn, Abū al-Jawzāʾ and Ibrāhīm an-Nakhaʿī held the same view as Ibn Masʿūd. **Sayyidnā ʿAbdullāh Ibn ʿAbbās** interpreted it of the face and palms, since a woman forced to go out by necessity finds these difficult to keep hidden while engaged in her work.

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān then offers the reconciliation of Qāḍī Bayḍāwī and Khāzin: nothing of the *zīnah* should be let show except what becomes uncovered in the course of working — which takes in the veil and sheet always, and the face and palms sometimes. That does not license men to look: where a woman is constrained to uncover her face or palms the men should turn their eyes away, unless a lawful act requires looking. Imām Mālik ruled that it is not allowed to see the face and palms of a non-mahram woman without lawful need, and Ibn Ḥajar Makkī quotes in his *Zawājir* that Imām ash-Shāfiʿī's view is the same, although the face and palms are not part of the *satr*. All sides agree, Maʿārif ul Qurʾān stresses, that where there is a risk of *fitnah* — the stirring of illicit desire — uncovering the face is not permitted; and since the face is the centre of beauty and attraction, it concludes that today the face should not be uncovered before non-mahram men except for medical treatment or in an emergency.

## "And let them draw their khimār over their juyūb"

*Khumur* is the plural of *khimār*, which Ibn Kathīr defines as what is used to cover the head. *Juyūb* is the plural of *jayb*, the upper opening of the garment just below the neck, which sits over the chest; so covering the *juyūb* means covering the neck and bosom. Saʿīd bin Jubayr explained "let them draw" (*wal-yaḍribna*) as: pull it around and tie it securely.

In pre-Islamic days, Maʿārif ul Qurʾān explains, women placed the sheet on the head and let its two sides hang down the back, leaving neck, ears and bosom uncovered; Ibn Kathīr describes the women of Jāhiliyyah passing in front of men with their chests, necks, forelocks, hair and earrings uncovered. The ayah does not introduce a new garment — it redirects one they already wore, bringing its two sides forward over the neck and bosom.

Al-Bukhārī recorded that Sayyidah ʿĀʾishah (may Allah be pleased with her) said: "May Allah have mercy on the women of the early emigrants. When Allah revealed the Ayah *and to draw their veils all over their Juyub*, they tore their aprons and Akhtamar themselves with them."

## The circle of those before whom there is no hijab

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān counts twelve exceptions in the verse: eight classes of mahram men, then four more. Allah has put into the hearts of close relatives a deep respect and honour for their womenfolk, so no mischief is expected from them; and since close relatives normally live together, daily convenience requires it. The eight are: husbands; fathers, including grandfathers and great-grandfathers; the husband's fathers and grandfathers; sons; the husband's sons by other wives; brothers, including half-brothers on either side — cousins are *not* included, they are non-mahram; brothers' sons; and sisters' sons.

This exemption is from *hijab*, not from *satr*. What a woman may not uncover in prayer she may not uncover before any mahram; only the husband is excepted there. And even with the husband, Maʿārif notes, looking at the private parts without need is not a preferable act; Sayyidah ʿĀʾishah said of the Prophet ﷺ, "Neither he saw my private parts nor did I see his."

Ibn al-Mundhir recorded that ʿIkrimah commented on this ayah that the paternal and maternal uncles are **not** mentioned, because they may describe a woman to their sons; so a woman should not remove her *khimār* in front of her paternal or maternal uncle. The same logic drives Ibn Kathīr's comment on "**or their women**": a woman may wear her adornment before other Muslim women, but not before the women of *Ahl adh-Dhimmah*, lest they describe her to their husbands — for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "No woman should describe another woman to her husband so that it is as if he is looking at her," recorded in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs from Ibn Masʿūd. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān records the dispute: Ibn Kathīr quotes Mujāhid that a Muslim woman may not uncover before non-Muslim women, yet there are ṣaḥīḥ ahadith showing that non-Muslim women used to visit the wives of the Prophet ﷺ; so some jurists treated non-Muslim women like non-mahram men, while Imām Rāzī held that "their women" covers Muslim and non-Muslim alike, the practice of the pious elders being desirable rather than obligatory — a view ʿAllāmah Ālūsī adopts in *Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī*.

"**Or their right hand possessions**" is read by Ibn Jarīr, and by Saʿīd bin al-Musayyib, of slave-women, including idolatresses. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān notes that many scholars restrict it to female slaves and not male ones, so that a woman must cover before a male slave as before any non-mahram; Sayyidnā ʿAbdullāh Ibn Masʿūd, Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and Ibn Sīrīn said a male slave may not see his female owner's hair.

"**The Tābiʿīn among men who have no desire**" — attendants and followers with no interest in women. ʿIkrimah said it refers to the hermaphrodite, and Ibn Kathīr reports the incident narrated in the Ṣaḥīḥ from ʿĀʾishah: such a person used to enter upon the family of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ until the Prophet ﷺ came in while he was describing a woman's figure in intimate detail, and said, "Lo! I think this person knows these things; he should never enter upon you." So the exemption is not about physical incapacity: Ibn Ḥajar Makkī comments in *Sharḥ al-Minhāj* that a man who is impotent, or lacking the organs, or very old is *not* included in this expression, and women must cover before all of them. What is meant, Maʿārif explains, is men of unsound mind with no sexual urge.

And "**children not yet aware of women's nakedness**" means, for Ibn Kathīr, the child too young to understand anything of women — their ʿawrah, their soft speech, their enticing ways of walking and moving. There is nothing wrong with such a small child entering upon women; but once a boy is adolescent or near it, able to tell who is beautiful from who is not, he should not enter upon women.

Ibn Kathīr closes the list with the hadith recorded in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs: "Avoid entering upon women." It was said, "O Messenger of Allah, what do you think about the male in-laws?" He said, "The male in-law is death."

## "And let them not stamp their feet"

Ibn Kathīr explains the practice being outlawed: during Jāhiliyyah, when women walked in the street wearing anklets that no one could hear, they would stamp their feet so that men could hear the anklets ringing. Allah forbade the believing women to do this — and by the same token, Ibn Kathīr adds, any movement that reveals a hidden adornment is forbidden. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān adds that putting something in the ornaments to make them sound, or striking them against one another, falls under the same ban.

Ibn Kathīr derives two further rulings. First, women should not go out wearing scent or perfume, lest men smell it: Abū ʿĪsā at-Tirmidhī recorded that Abū Mūsā (may Allah be pleased with him) said that the Prophet ﷺ said, "Every eye commits fornication and adultery, and when a woman puts on perfume and passes through a gathering, she is such and such" — meaning an adulteress. Second, women are forbidden to walk in the middle of the street, because of the wanton display it involves: Abū Dāwūd recorded that Abū Usayd al-Anṣārī heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, as he came out of the Masjid and men and women were mixing in the street, tell the women, "Keep back, for you have no right to walk in the middle of the street. You should keep to the sides of the road."

Imām Jaṣṣāṣ argued from the same verse that if even the sound of ornaments counts as exposing *zīnah*, then going out in a decorated veil is unlawful all the more. Some jurists pressed the inference further, to a woman's voice — hence Ibn al-Humām including the voice in *satr* on the basis of *Nawāzil*, and the Ḥanafī ruling that the adhān by a woman is *makrūh*. But the books of Imām ash-Shāfiʿī do not count the voice as part of *satr*, and it is established by hadith that the wives of the Prophet ﷺ used to speak with non-mahrams from behind the curtain even after hijab was revealed. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān's conclusion, following Jaṣṣāṣ, is that hearing a woman's voice is impermissible only where it may create *fitnah*; where there is no such apprehension it is allowed — though the prudent course is to avoid unnecessary conversation with non-mahrams. And Allah knows best.

## Living it

The closing words are addressed to everyone together: **"And all of you beg Allah to forgive you all, O believers, that you may be successful."** After the separate instructions to men and to women comes a combined one, Maʿārif ul Qurʾān explains, because sexual desire is a delicate thing that stays concealed from other people — but everything, concealed or open, is completely known to Allah. So whoever has erred in these injunctions should beg Allah's pardon, feel repentant over what has passed, and make a firm resolve not to return to it. Ibn Kathīr puts it from the other side: practise what you are commanded of these beautiful manners and praiseworthy characteristics, give up the evil ways of the people of Jāhiliyyah, and know that the greatest success is in doing what Allah and His Messenger ﷺ command and avoiding what He forbids. And Allah is the source of strength.

passages.title: Marriage, chastity, and freeing bondservants
passages.tafsir:
Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene: Sūrah an-Nūr carries mostly the injunctions that protect chastity and prevent shamelessness. Now Allah opens the lawful door: marry, and marry off those in your care; if you cannot yet, stay chaste and wait; and where a person is held in bondage, write the contract that leads to freedom, and never push her into the very sin the sūrah has been sealing off.

**What holds them together.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it precisely: Islamic law is built on the precept of moderation, so its rulings stay in touch with natural human feeling. When it is enjoined to desist strictly from unlawful lust, it becomes equally important to provide a lawful access for those same natural desires — and in the terminology of Qur'an and Sunnah that path is called *nikāḥ* (marriage). Ibn Kathir says these clear ayat contain "a group of unambiguous rulings and firm commands": marry them off, stay chaste, write the freedom contract, do not coerce — each tied to a promise or a mercy.

## Ayah 32: "Marry off the single among you"

**The word *al-ayāmā*.** Ibn Kathir explains that *al-ayāmā* is the plural of *ayyim*, used for a woman who has no husband and a man who has no wife — whether they were married before and then separated, or were never married at all. He cites al-Jawharī reporting this from the scholars of the Arabic language; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same. So this is not only about getting young people married: it sweeps in the widow, the widower, the divorced.

**Notice who is addressed.** The verb is plural: *marry them off*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that scholars and jurists are unanimous that, from this manner of address, the preferable and *masnūn* way (in keeping with the Prophet's ﷺ practice) is that marriages be arranged through guardians. Imam Abū Ḥanīfah and some other Imams held that this describes a *sunnah* and the preferred way: if an adult woman marries a man within her own *kufʼ* (a suitable match) without her guardian's permission, the marriage is proper, though she is blameworthy for acting against the sunnah. Imam ash-Shāfiʿī and some other Imams held such a marriage null and void. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's own reading: the ayah establishes that guardian mediation is *preferable*, but is silent on the status of a marriage contracted without it — and *ayāmā* covers adult men too, whose marriages all agree are valid without a guardian.

**"And the righteous among your bondmen and bondwomen."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes *ṣāliḥīn* here in its literal sense — those with the means and capacity to marry: able to fulfil a wife's conjugal rights and to pay maintenance and the prompt dower.

Some jurists held that if such a servant shows the need and desire to marry, it is binding on the owner to marry him or her off; the majority ruled that what binds the owner is to place *no hindrance* in the way, since a bondservant's marriage could not be concluded without the owner's permission. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites the Prophet's ﷺ words, recorded by Tirmidhī: if someone of that kind comes to you with a proposal and you like his morals, then marry him off — and if you do not, great mischief will be created on earth.

**"If they are poor, Allah will enrich them out of His bounty."** ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah reported from Ibn ʿAbbās: "Allah encouraged them to get married, commanded both free men and servants to get married, and He promised to enrich them." Ibn Masʿūd said, "Seek the richness through marriage," reciting this phrase — recorded by Ibn Jarīr, with something similar recorded by al-Baghawī from ʿUmar. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported Abū Bakr addressing the Muslims: follow Allah's injunction to marry, and He will fulfil His promise of granting riches.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the other edge: good news for the poor Muslim who wants to marry to secure his religion but has no means — and advice to anyone who would turn down a proposal because of a man's present circumstances. Wealth does not always stay; the merit of the person is the thing that matters.

Ibn Kathir illustrates it with a marriage the Prophet ﷺ himself performed, for a man who owned nothing but his waist wrap and could not even buy a ring made of iron; he ﷺ married him to the woman anyway, making her *mahr* (dower) his promise to teach her whatever he knew of the Qur'an. And it is known from the generosity and kindness of Allah, Ibn Kathir adds, that He provided what was sufficient for her and for him.

Tafsīr Mazharī attaches a condition — the one marrying must intend to safeguard his chastity and to follow the sunnah, and after that place his trust and faith in Allah.

The ayah closes: **Allah is All-Sufficient, All-Knowing.**

## The ruling on marriage itself

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out the whole scale:

- **Obligatory** — where a person has a strong apprehension that without marriage he will not be able to keep the prescribed limits of the Sharīʿah and will fall into sin, *and* he has the means. Jurists are almost all unanimous on this; as long as he does not marry, he remains sinful.
- **Prohibited or unbecoming** — where someone has a strong notion that marrying will itself lead him into sin, for instance that he is not capable of meeting his wife's conjugal rights.
- **The even case** — no strong risk either way. Imam Abū Ḥanīfah held that marrying is better than occupying that time with extra prayers; Imam ash-Shāfiʿī held that occupation in prayers is preferable.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the reasoning behind that last difference: marriage is in itself a lawful act, and the element of worship enters it indirectly — one is saved from sin by it, and righteous children add to one's reward — so Imam ash-Shāfiʿī gave direct worship precedence. Imam Abū Ḥanīfah held that the element of worship is greater in marriage than in other lawful acts, since many authentic ahadith emphasise it repeatedly as a practice of the Messengers — which no hadith says of eating, drinking or sleeping. Tafsīr Mazharī offers a middle position: if a man judges that household life will not hinder his worship and remembrance of Allah, marrying is preferable for him; but if he has a hunch that marriage will hinder Allah's remembrance, then abstaining for worship is preferable — "let not your possessions nor your children divert you from Allah's remembrance" (63:9).

**From the Sunnah.** The Prophet ﷺ said: "O young men, whoever among you can afford to get married, let him marry, for it is more effective in lowering the gaze and protecting the private parts. Whoever cannot do that, then let him fast, for it is a protection for him." Ibn Kathir records this in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs from the hadith of Ibn Masʿūd. And in the Sunan, recorded from more than one person: "Marry and have children, for I will be proud of you before the nations on the Day of Resurrection."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates from the Musnad of Aḥmad that the Prophet ﷺ asked ʿAkkāf whether he had a wife — no — and whether he had the means — yes; and told him that in that case he was a brother of Shayṭān, for our sunnah is to get married. The majority of jurists, Maʿārif notes, hold such narrations to apply to the case where abstaining carries a predominant risk of sin.

## Ayah 33: chastity in the waiting

**"And let those who do not find the means to marry keep themselves chaste, until Allah enriches them of His bounty."** Ibn Kathir reads this as a direct command to those who do not have the means: they are to keep themselves chaste *and* avoid what is unlawful, with fasting the prescribed means. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the man who, if he married now, would risk failing his wife's rights and becoming sinful; he too waits with patience, keeping fasts abundantly, until Allah grants him out of His bounty enough to afford it.

ʿIkrimah gave that work a concrete picture: a man sees a woman and it is as if he feels desire; if he has a wife, let him go to her and fulfil his desire with her, and if he has no wife, "then let him ponder the kingdom of heaven and earth until Allah grants him means of livelihood."

## The contract of freedom (*al-kitābah*)

**"And such of your servants as seek a writing of emancipation, give them such writing, if you find that there is good and honesty in them."** Ibn Kathir: this is a command from Allah to slave-owners — if their servants ask them for a contract of emancipation, they should write it for them, provided the servant has some skill and means of earning so that he can pay what the contract stipulates.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes the mechanism. The servant asks his owner to fix an amount by mutual consent, which he earns by his labour and pays; the owner may equally initiate the deal. Once struck it becomes binding under Islamic law and the owner has no authority to call it off; the moment the agreed payment is complete, freedom takes effect automatically. The sum is called *badal al-kitābah*, and Islamic law has fixed no limit on it — whatever the two agree on is what stands.

**Obligatory or recommended?** Ibn Kathir cites al-Bukhārī reporting that Ibn Jurayj asked ʿAṭāʼ whether an owner who knows his servant has money is obliged to write him a contract of emancipation, and ʿAṭāʼ answered, "I do not think it can be anything but obligatory." That exchange with ʿAṭāʼ was also narrated by ʿAbdur-Razzāq. Attached to it in al-Bukhārī's version is the account of Sīrīn, who had a lot of money and asked Anas for a contract of emancipation and was refused; he went to ʿUmar bin al-Khaṭṭāb, who told Anas, "Write it for him," and when Anas still refused, ʿUmar hit him with his whip and recited, "give them such writing, if you find that there is good and honesty in them" — then Anas wrote the contract. Ibn Kathir notes that al-Bukhārī mentioned this with a disconnected chain. Against the view that it is obligatory, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that jurists commonly — including the author of *Hidāyah* — take the instruction as recommendatory: not compulsory for the owner to agree, yet preferable, and bringing good reward.

**"If you find that there is good (*khayr*) in them."** Ibn Kathir reports three explanations from the early scholars: trustworthiness; honesty; a skill and the ability to earn. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports from ʿAbdullāh Ibn ʿUmar and many other scholars that *khayr* means the strength to earn — without it the servant's labour is wasted and the owner suffers loss too — and from other scholars that it means there should be no risk of harm to the Muslims from his freedom; Tafsīr Mazharī concludes that the word carries both meanings at once.

**"And give them out of the wealth of Allah which He has given you."** Ibn Kathir records two readings. Al-Ḥasan, ʿAbdur-Raḥmān bin Zayd bin Aslam and his father, and Muqātil bin Ḥayyān held this to be the share of Zakāh that Allah stated to be these servants' right — the view Ibn Jarīr favoured. Ibrāhīm an-Nakhaʿī said it is urging the people, their masters and others alike, and this was also the view of Buraydah bin al-Ḥuṣayb al-Aslamī and Qatādah; Ibn ʿAbbās said simply: "Allah commanded the believers to help in freeing slaves." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān harmonises them — the address is to Muslims in general and owners in particular, so the community may help from Zakāh money, while owners are induced to contribute on their own or reduce the agreed sum — and records that it was the practice of the Companions to reduce the amount by a third or a fourth.

The essence of the whole ruling, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, is to open up the doors of freedom: freeing a slave is a common injunction across the law's expiations, and this contract is one such route. Maʿārif also pauses on the wording — the wealth *of Allah* which He has given *you* — and draws three things from it: Allah is the real owner of everything; He has given man possession of certain things by His grace; and restrictions come with that possession, some spending prohibited, some obligatory, some preferable.

Ibn Kathir brings the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, recorded by Imām Aḥmad, at-Tirmidhī, an-Nasāʼī and Ibn Mājah, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "There are three whom it is a right upon Allah to help: one who gets married seeking chastity; a slave who makes a contract with his master with the aim of buying his freedom; and one who fights for the sake of Allah." Two of the three are exactly the people of this passage: the one marrying for chastity in ayah 32, and the one buying his freedom in ayah 33.

## "And force not your slave-girls to prostitution"

**The occasion of revelation.** Ibn Kathir explains the practice: among the people of the Jāhiliyyah there were some who, having a slave-girl, would send her out to commit zinā and charge money for it. When Islam came, Allah forbade the believers to do that. According to the reports of a number of earlier and later scholars of tafsir, the ayah was revealed concerning ʿAbdullāh bin Ubayy bin Salūl, who had slave-girls he forced into prostitution so that he could take their earnings and because he wanted them to have children who would enhance his status.

Al-Aʿmash narrated from Abū Sufyān that Jābir said it was revealed about a slave-girl of ʿAbdullāh bin Ubayy named Musaykah, whom he used to force into immoral actions though she refused; an-Nasāʼī also records something similar. Muqātil bin Ḥayyān said he had heard — and Allah knows best — that it was revealed about two men who forced two slave-girls of theirs, Musaykah and her mother Umaymah, and that the two women came to the Prophet ﷺ and told him about what was being done to them. Then Allah revealed the ayah.

Two women who were owned, with nothing to bargain with, brought their complaint to the Prophet ﷺ — and the answer came down on their side.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds why an explicit command was needed: this was an entrenched pre-Islamic custom, and once Islam placed strict punishments on adultery — on free and slave alike — special strict orders were required to uproot it.

**"If they desire chastity."** Ibn Kathir reads this as: if they want to be chaste — which, he adds, is the case with the majority of slave-girls. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān guards the clause against misuse: although the wording is conditional, there is consensus of the Ummah that this is not permission to press a woman who has not expressed such a wish.
