In the pre-Islamic days obscenity was so common that these women had not minded it; after the coming of Islam they repented and wished to be out of it, and their owners still forced them. The condition is a rebuke, not a loophole.

**"That you may make a gain in the goods of this worldly life."** Ibn Kathir: from the money they earn and their children. He notes that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade the money earned by the cupper, the prostitute and the fortune-teller, and that according to another report the earnings of a prostitute are evil, the earnings of a cupper are evil, and the price of a dog is evil. Wealth built on her body is filth.

**"But if anyone compels them, then after such compulsion Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful."** Ibn Kathir states that the forgiveness is *towards them* — towards the coerced women. Ibn Abī Ṭalḥah narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās: "If you do that, then Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful, and their sin will be on the one who forced them to do that." Mujāhid, ʿAṭāʼ al-Khurāsānī, al-Aʿmash and Qatādah held the same view, and Tafsīr Mazharī, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates it, says the same: Allah pardons her sin, and that sin passes to the one who compelled her.

## Ayah 34: the seal

"And indeed We have sent down for you Ayat that make things plain, and the example of those who passed away before you, and an admonition for those who have Taqwa."

Ibn Kathir unpacks the three:

- **Ayat that make things plain** — in the Qur'an there are ayat which are clear and explain matters in detail.
- **The example of those who passed away** — reports about the nations of the past and what happened to them when they went against the commandments of Allah, as Allah says, "And We made them a precedent, and an example to later generations" (43:56); a rebuke for committing sin and forbidden deeds.
- **An admonition for those who have taqwā** — meaning, Ibn Kathir says, those who remember and fear Allah. The same clarity falls on everyone; only the Allah-conscious are actually admonished by it.

## Living it

- **Marriage is a communal concern.** Ayah 32 addresses the community about its unmarried — widowed and divorced included, since they fall inside *al-ayāmā*. Who nearby is being left to wait?
- **Do not let poverty veto a proposal** — wealth does not always stay; merit is the thing to weigh.
- **If you cannot marry yet, seek chastity actively** — fasting, and ʿIkrimah's counsel to turn the gaze upward to the kingdom of heaven and earth until Allah opens the way.
- **Never obstruct someone's path out** — a guardian delaying a marriage, an owner delaying a freedom contract. And remember whose money you hold: "the wealth of Allah which He has given you" comes with conditions, one of them being to spend it setting people free.

passages.title: Allah is the Light: the lamp and its houses
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat move from the highest reality to the most ordinary street: Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth, then one of the Qur'an's most famous parables, then where that light is found: in the chests of men who hear the call to prayer with money still in their hands and go anyway. Ibn Kathir states the thread plainly: having likened the believer's heart to a lamp lit with good oil in a clear glass, Allah states where it belongs — the Masjids, the places on earth most beloved to Him.

## "Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth"

**How the early authorities read "Light".** 'Ali bin Abi Talhah reported from Ibn 'Abbas that this means: the Guide of the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth. Ibn Jurayj reports Mujahid and Ibn 'Abbas saying that He is controlling their affairs — their stars, their sun and moon. As-Suddi said: by His Light the heavens and the earth are illuminated.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the linguistic care. Imam Ghazali defined *nūr*, light, as that which is bright and manifest on its own and makes other things bright and evident. So the word cannot be used of Allah in its literal sense, since He is free of body and materiality. There is consensus among the scholars, Maʿārif reports, that *nūr* here carries the sense of *Munawwir*, the One who brightens. The light intended is the light of guidance.

In the Two Sahihs — al-Bukhari and Muslim — Ibn 'Abbas reported that when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ rose to pray at night he would say: *"O Allah, to You be praise, You are the Sustainer of heaven and earth and whoever is in them. To You be praise, You are the Light of the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them."* And Ibn Mas'ud said: "There is no night or day with your Lord; the Light of the Throne comes from the Light of His Face."

**Whose light is the parable about?** Ibn Kathir records two views on the pronoun in *mathalu nūrihi*, "the parable of **His** light". The first, Ibn 'Abbas's, refers it to Allah: the parable of His guidance in the heart of the believer. The second refers it to the believer: his heart together with the guidance he is naturally inclined to and the Qur'an he learns.

Ibn Jarir reports from Ubayy bin Ka'b that this is the believer in whose heart Allah has laid the light of faith and of the Qur'an: Allah began with His own light and then mentioned the light of the believer, and Ubayy used to recite the phrase as *mathalu nūri man āmana bihi*, "the parable of the light of the one who believes in Him". Maʿārif notes that Sa'id bin Jubayr reported the same from Ibn 'Abbas. The two views do not compete: the light is Allah's; the lamp is the believer's chest.

## The parable, piece by piece

**The niche (mishkāt).** Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Muhammad bin Ka'b and others said this refers to the position of the wick in the lamp; it was also said that the niche is a niche in the house. Maʿārif gives the mapping: the believer's chest is the niche, and his heart set within it is the lamp.

**The lamp (miṣbāḥ).** Ibn Kathir: this is the flame that burns brightly, the parable Allah gives of obedience to Him — Allah calls obedience light. Ubayy bin Ka'b said, "The lamp is the light, and this refers to the Qur'an and the faith that is in his heart." As-Suddi said, "It is the lamp."

**The glass (zujājah).** Ubayy bin Ka'b and others said this is the likeness of the believer's heart — which in its purity and clarity, as Ibn Kathir puts it, is like a lamp in transparent, jewel-like glass, while the Qur'an and Shari'ah by which it is guided are like good, pure, shining oil in which there is no impurity or deviation.

**The blessed olive, "neither of the east nor of the west".** Ibn Kathir makes this concrete: the tree is not in the eastern part of the land, where it would get no sun in the first part of the day, nor in the western part, where it would be shaded before sunset — it is in a central position where it gets sun from the beginning of the day until the end, so its oil is good and pure and shining. Ibn Abi Hatim records Ibn 'Abbas saying, "This is a tree in the desert which is not shaded by any other tree or mountain or cave, nothing covers it, and this is best for its oil" — nothing has come between this tree and the light.

**"Whose oil would almost glow forth, though no fire touched it."** 'Abdur-Rahman bin Zayd bin Aslam said the oil itself is shining. Maʿārif reads the transparent olive oil as the natural light of guidance deposited in a person's nature, which carries the inherent capability to accept the truth — and just as olive oil produces brightness when the flame is set to it, so that natural light in the believer's heart, when it joins the message and knowledge of Allah, is brightened and brightens the world.

Maʿārif observes that the Companions confined this parable to the believer's heart because it is only the believer who draws benefit from this light. The natural light placed in human hearts at creation is not confined to believers; it is part of the instinct of every human being. That is why in every corner of the world you find people who believe in the existence of Allah and turn towards Him, however many errors they make in conceiving of Him. A *ṣaḥīḥ* hadith endorses this: every child is born upon the natural instinct (*fiṭrah*), and it is his parents who afterwards put him on the wrong path.

**"Light upon Light."** Al-'Awfi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that this means the faith and deeds of a person. As-Suddi gave the image that unlocks the parable: "Light of the fire and the light of the oil: when they are combined they give light, and neither of them can give light without the other. Similarly the light of the Qur'an and the light of faith give light when they are combined, and neither can do so without the other." Oil never lit stays dark; a flame with no oil dies.

**"Allah guides to His Light whom He wills."** Ibn Kathir: Allah shows the way to the ones whom He chooses. Maʿārif points out the movement across the ayah: at the beginning, the bestowal of light is common to everyone in the heavens and the earth; at the end it narrows. The first is the light given to human nature at birth; the second is the Qur'anic light, which not everyone attains — only those granted divine help.

Ibn Kathir cites the hadith recorded by Imam Ahmad from 'Abdullah bin 'Amr, who said, "I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: *'Allah created His creation in darkness, then on the same day He sent His Light upon them. Whoever was touched by His Light on that day will be guided and whoever was missed will be led astray. Hence I say: the pens have dried in accordance with the knowledge of Allah, may He be glorified.'*" The ayah closes, "And Allah sets forth parables for mankind, and Allah is All-Knower of everything" — meaning, says Ibn Kathir, He knows best who deserves to be guided and who deserves to be led astray.

**Which heart is yours?** Imam Ahmad recorded from Abu Sa'id Al-Khudri that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"Hearts are of four kinds: the heart that is clear like a shining lamp; the heart that is covered and tied up; the heart that is upside-down; and the heart that is clad in armour. As for the clear heart, it is the heart of the believer in which is a lamp filled with light; as for the covered heart, this is the heart of the disbeliever; as for the upside-down heart, this is the heart of the hypocrite, who recognises then denies; as for the armour-clad heart, this is the heart in which there is both faith and hypocrisy. The parable of the faith in it is that of a sprout irrigated with good water, and the likeness of the hypocrisy in it is that of sores fed by blood and pus. Whichever of the two prevails is the characteristic that will dominate."* Ibn Kathir notes that its chain of narrators is good (*jayyid*), although al-Bukhari and Muslim did not record it.

## Where the lamp belongs

Grammatically, *fī buyūt*, "in houses", connects back to "Allah guides to His Light whom He wills" — the reading Maʿārif attributes to Ibn Kathir. There is consensus among the commentators, Maʿārif says, that "houses" here means the mosques. Abu Hayyan, in *Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ*, notes that the wording is general: it takes in houses set aside for teaching the Qur'an too.

**"Which Allah has permitted to be raised."** *Adhina* comes from *idhn*, permission; the scholars are unanimous, Maʿārif reports, that it is used here for a command. *Rūḥ al-Maʿānī* draws out the subtlety: the aim is to train the believers to be so ready for whatever pleases Allah that they need no order at all — they wait only for permission, and the moment they are given leave, they hurry to carry it out.

*Turfaʿa* comes from *rafʿ*, to raise, uplift or exalt, and the sources keep both senses. 'Ikrimah and Mujahid took it as building the mosques, as the Qur'an speaks of Ibrahim raising the foundations of the House (2:127). Hasan al-Basri gave a different view: the word is used for respecting and venerating mosques and keeping them clean of filthy things. Ibn 'Abbas explained that Allah has forbidden idle talk and absurd conduct in them. Maʿārif concludes that the word encompasses both: build them, and honour them — which is why the Prophet ﷺ prohibited coming to the mosque with the smell of onions or garlic on the breath.

**From the Sunnah.** 'Uthman bin 'Affan heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say, *"Whoever builds a Masjid seeking the Face of Allah, Allah will build for him something similar to it in Paradise"* — narrated in the Two Sahihs. And 'A'ishah said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded us to build Masjids among the houses, and to clean them and perfume them" — recorded by Ahmad and the Sunan compilers except an-Nasa'i.

But building is not display. Abu Dawud narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, *"I was not commanded to* Tashyīd *the Masjids"* — which Ibn 'Abbas glossed as decorating them the way the Jews and Christians did. Maʿārif gives the counterweight: 'Uthman used hard wood in rebuilding the Prophet's mosque to give it an impressive look, and 'Umar ibn 'Abdul 'Aziz later improved it further, with no one objecting. Imam Abu Hanifa ruled that where there is no ostentation and the intent is to venerate His house, there is no objection to fine construction.

**The reward of going.** It is confirmed in the Two Sahihs that a man's prayer in congregation is twenty-five times better than his prayer in his house or the marketplace — because when he goes out to the mosque for no purpose but the prayer, he does not take a single step without being raised one level in status and having one sin removed. And the Sunan record: *"Those who walk to the Masjids when it is dark, give them the glad tidings of complete Light on the Day of Resurrection."* Notice how exactly that answers the parable: the man carrying his small lamp through dark streets is promised perfect light on the Day it matters.

**"In them His Name is remembered."** Ibn 'Abbas said this means that His Book is recited therein. Maʿārif takes the expression broadly: all kinds of remembrance — voluntary prayers, recitation of the Qur'an, learning Islamic teachings, sermons, lectures on the Shari'ah. And *bi'l-ghuduwwi wa'l-āṣāl*, "in the mornings and in the evenings", means, as Maʿārif puts it, that He is worshipped there all the time.

## The men who carry the lamp

Now the passage names the people: *rijāl*, men whom neither trade (*tijārah*) nor sale (*bayʿ*) diverts from the remembrance of Allah, nor from establishing the prayer, nor from giving the zakah.

**Why both words?** Since "sale" is already included in "trade", Maʿārif reports that some commentators take *tijārah* here as purchase only; others explain the separate mention of *bayʿ* like this: trade at large has a wide scope in which profits come after a long wait, whereas by selling something one receives the money immediately, in cash. These men do not weigh even the most immediate worldly gain against the prayer.

Ibn Kathir sets the ayah beside its companions: "O you who believe! Let not your properties or your children divert you from the remembrance of Allah" (63:9), and "When the call is proclaimed for the Salah on Friday, hasten earnestly to the remembrance of Allah and leave off business" (62:9). They know that what is with Him is better than what they possess, because what they have is transient and what is with Allah is eternal.

**The scene behind the words.** It was reported from Salim that his father 'Abdullah bin 'Umar was in the marketplace when the *iqāmah* was called and the traders shut their stores and went into the mosque; Ibn 'Umar said, "Concerning them this ayah was revealed" (recorded by Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Jarir). Qurtubi preserves a sharper image: two Companions in the Prophet's own time, a trader and a blacksmith. When the call reached the trader mid-weighing, he would leave everything and get up for the mosque. When it reached the blacksmith with his hammer raised over hot iron, he would drop the hammer without completing the stroke.

*Rūḥ al-Maʿānī* observes that the verse points out that most of the Companions were traders or manufacturers, because the quality praised here can only belong to those in trade and sales who do not let their profession interfere with the remembrance of Allah. The virtue is not withdrawal from the world; it is that the world does not set the timetable.

**How far does "diverts" reach?** 'Ali bin Abi Talhah reported Ibn 'Abbas as saying it means diverted from the prescribed prayers — also the view of Muqatil bin Hayyan and ar-Rabi' bin Anas. As-Suddi said: from the prayer in congregation. Ibn Kathir sums up the character: they give priority to obeying Allah and what pleases Him over doing what they themselves want.

Maʿārif reads *rijāl*, "men", as a hint that it is men whose presence is required in the mosques, and that for women it is better to pray at home, citing the hadith related in the Musnad of Ahmad and by al-Bayhaqi from Umm Salamah that the best mosques for women are the secluded corners of their homes.

**"They fear a Day when hearts and eyes will be overturned."** This is the Day of Resurrection, says Ibn Kathir, when hearts and eyes will be overturned because of the intensity of the fear and terror of that Day — as in "And warn them of the Day that is drawing near" (40:18) and "but He gives them respite up to a Day when the eyes will stare in horror" (14:42). He sets beside it Surah al-Insan on those who give food, despite loving it, to the poor, the orphan and the captive, saying, "We feed you seeking Allah's Face only. Verily, We fear from our Lord a Day, hard and distressful" — and Allah saves them from the evil of that Day and rewards their patience with Paradise and silken garments (76:8–12).

Maʿārif makes the point precisely: this is the last of their qualities, and the most telling. Despite being busy with Allah's obedience and worship all the time, they do not count themselves safe; the fear of the reckoning is constantly in their minds — and that fear is itself the fruit of the light of guidance Allah granted them in the ayah before.

## What the lamp is worth

*"That Allah may reward them according to the best of their deeds"* — Ibn Kathir: these are the ones from whom the best of their deeds is accepted and whose evil deeds are overlooked.

*"And add even more for them out of His grace"* — He accepts their good deeds and multiplies them, as Allah says that He does not wrong even the weight of a speck of dust (4:40), that whoever brings a good deed shall have ten times the like of it (6:160), and that He gives manifold increase to whom He wills (2:261). Maʿārif: their reward does not end with the recompense earned by their actions; something extra is given on His own.

*"And Allah provides without measure to whom He wills"* — as Maʿārif puts it, Allah is bound by no rule, nor does His treasure ever run down. The lamp is small and the oil is a jar; the giving is without a ledger.

## Living it

The oil is the natural light of guidance placed in you at birth — the inborn capacity to accept truth, which almost glows on its own. The fire is revelation. Neither lights the room alone; that is As-Suddi's point, and it is the hinge of the whole parable. So the practical question is not "am I decent by nature" but "have I brought the Qur'an to the disposition Allah gave me" — and then, keep the glass clean, since the light shines through a heart that is clear, not one covered, or turned upside-down, or half-clad in armour. The passage puts that light exactly where you live it: in the mosque you build, honour, and keep quiet; and in the moment the call goes out while your hand is on the scale, or on the hammer.

Maʿārif tells us what comes next. Ayat 39 and 40 turn to those who were given the light of guidance in their nature but turned away when Allah's revelation came to kindle it, and so remained in darkness — their deeds likened to a mirage that looks like water until the thirsty man reaches it and finds nothing; and to darkness upon darkness in a deep sea, where a man who puts out his hand cannot see it. There is light that is oil and flame together, and there is the illusion of light. It is worth knowing which one you are walking towards.

passages.title: The disbelievers' deeds: mirage and layered darkness
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat are the shadow that falls after the description of the believers. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that up to this point the passage has been describing the righteous believers, "whose chests are the niches for the Nur of guidance" — the light of guidance — and who readily accept that light. Now Allah draws two portraits of what a life looks like when that light is refused: a mirage that promises water and delivers nothing, and a sea so deep and so layered with darkness that a man cannot see his own hand. What holds ayah 39 and ayah 40 together is that both answer the same question — *what happens to the deeds of a person who rejects Allah?* One answer is: they turn out to be nothing. The other is: the man never even knew where he was going.

## Where we are in the surah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out how ayah 38 closes the description of the believers: they will be graced with the best reward for their actions, "and will give them more out of His grace" — their recompense does not stop at what their deeds strictly earned; Allah adds something extra from Himself. And "Allah gives whom He wills without counting," meaning that Allah is bound by no rule and His treasure never runs low; He grants unlimited provision to whomever He wills.

Then the camera turns. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān frames ayat 39–40 like this: these are people who were given, in their very nature, the Nur of guidance by Allah; but when Allah's revelation reached them to light them up, they turned away to reject it, and so lost that light and stayed in the darkness. That is the tragedy the two parables illustrate.

## Two parables, because there are two kinds of people

Ibn Kathir opens by noting the structure: these are **two examples which Allah sets forth of two kinds of disbelievers**. He observes that this is a pattern in the Qur'an. At the beginning of Sūrat al-Baqarah, Allah sets forth two parables of the hypocrites — one involving fire and the other involving water. In Sūrat ar-Raʿd He again gives two parables, this time of the guidance and knowledge instilled in the heart, again involving fire and water. Ibn Kathir adds that he has discussed each of them in its own place and sees no need to repeat it here.

Who exactly are the two groups? The two commentaries in front of us divide them a little differently, and both readings are worth holding.

**Ibn Kathir** takes the first parable — the mirage — to describe the disbelievers who *call others* to their disbelief, thinking that they have good actions and beliefs when this is not in fact the case. This, he says, is the parable of one whose ignorance is deep and advanced. The second parable — the dark sea — he takes to describe those whose ignorance is *simple*: those who are uneducated and foolish and blindly follow the leaders of disbelief, knowing and understanding nothing.

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** divides them by belief in the Hereafter. The first category believes in the Day of Judgement and the Hereafter, and has faith that some of their good acts, according to their own reckoning, will be rewarded there — these are the people of the mirage, because they at least have an image of something ahead of them, even if it is only an image. The second category are those who do not believe in the Hereafter and the Day of Judgement at all — and so, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, they are deprived of even the *illusive* Nur that the first group had. The first group at least laboured under the illusion that they had done some good deeds which would help them in the Hereafter; the second did not deem it necessary to work for a Hereafter they did not believe in. Hence they will have nothing but darkness, and complete darkness, with them on that Day.

Both readings land in the same place: a life can be full of activity and still be empty of anything that survives.

## Ayah 39: the mirage

The word the Qur'an uses for the ground here is **qīʿah**. Ibn Kathir explains it as a vast, flat, level area of land in which the mirage may appear — exactly the kind of open plain on which a mirage appears. It matters that the ground is level and featureless: there is nothing on it to break the illusion, nothing to give the eye a second opinion. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes it plainly: in a level plain the shining sand creates the illusion of water from a distance.

Ibn Kathir adds a detail that shows how closely the early scholars had looked at the phenomenon: there are different kinds of mirage — one which appears after midday, and another which appears in the morning and looks like water between heaven and earth.

Then notice who is walking toward it. Not a casual traveller: **the thirsty one**. This is not a man idly mistaken; it is a man whose life depends on the thing he thinks he sees. As Ibn Kathir puts it, a person who is in need of water sees the mirage, thinks that it is water, and heads towards it in order to drink from it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān carries the picture to its end: as the thirsty person approaches, the illusion disappears, leaving him completely exhausted, and he ultimately dies of thirst.

**"He finds it to be nothing."** Ibn Kathir applies this directly: similarly, the disbeliever thinks that he is doing something good and that he has achieved something — but when Allah judges him on the Day of Resurrection, brings him to account and examines his deeds, he will find that *nothing* has been accepted at all. Ibn Kathir names the two reasons a deed fails this test: either because of a lack of sincere belief, or because he did not follow the proper ways of the Sharīʿah — the law and way Allah revealed. Intention and method: a deed needs both, and the mirage is what a deed looks like when it has neither.

He brings another ayah as a parallel: "And We shall turn to whatever deeds they did, and We shall make such deeds as scattered floating particles of dust" (25:23). Particles of dust in a shaft of light — visible, countless, and weightless.

Ibn Kathir notes that a similar view was also narrated from **Ubayy bin Kaʿb, Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Qatādah** and others.

**What he does find.** The most arresting turn in ayah 39 is that the man does not simply find nothing. He finds *Allah* there — "but he finds Allah with him, Who will pay him his due. And Allah is swift in taking account." He ran toward what he assumed was water and arrived instead at his Reckoning. The one thing he was not expecting to meet was the one thing actually waiting. And there is no reprieve of delay: Allah is swift in taking account.

## A report from the Two Sahihs

At this point in his commentary Ibn Kathir cites a report **in the Two Sahihs** that on the Day of Resurrection it will be said to the Jews, "What did you used to worship?" They will say, "We used to worship ʿUzayr the son of Allah." It will be said to them, "You have lied. Allah has not begotten a son. What do you want?" They will say, "O Lord, we are thirsty, give us something to drink." It will be said to them, "Do you not see?" Then Hell will be shown to them as if it is a mirage, parts of it consuming other parts, and they will go and fall into it.

The image of the mirage appears inside the report itself, in the words of the report: what they are shown is Hell, and it is shown to them *as if it is a mirage*. Their stated need is thirst, and what answers it is the Fire.

## Ayah 40: darkness upon darkness

The second parable moves from blinding light to no light at all: "Or like the darkness in a vast deep sea, overwhelmed with waves topped by waves, topped by dark clouds, darkness upon darkness: if a man stretches out his hand, he can hardly see it."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes the layers in order, and the order is the point. **In the first place it is dark because of its depth.** Then it is covered by a big wave. Then that wave is itself enshrouded by another wave. And over that there is a mass of dark cloud. Each layer would be enough to blind a man on its own; here they are stacked. In short, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sums it up, there is darkness over darkness — so much so that if someone takes out his hand, he cannot have even a glimpse of it.

The final touch is the most human one: if he stretches out his hand, he can hardly see it. Ibn Kathir's comment is simply that he can hardly see it *because it is so intensely dark*. Not a distant landmark, not the shore — his own hand, at arm's length. A man in that state has lost not only the destination but himself.

**Whose heart is this?** Ibn Kathir says this is the parable of the heart of the disbeliever whose ignorance is simple: the one who merely follows, and does not know the true nature of the one whom he follows or where he is going. He illustrates it with the ignorant man in the parable who was asked, "Where are you going?" He said, "With them." He was asked, "Where are they going?" He said, "I do not know." Two questions were enough to expose an entire life. It is worth sitting with, because this is the least dramatic form of misguidance: not a decision, but a drift.

**Ubayy bin Kaʿb** said of "darkness upon darkness" that such a person is enveloped in *five* types of darkness: his speech is darkness, his deeds are darkness, his coming in is darkness, his going out is darkness, and his destiny on the Day of Resurrection will be darkness in the fire of Hell. Ibn Kathir notes that **as-Suddī** and **ar-Rabīʿ bin Anas** also said something similar. Notice the reach of that list — words, actions, entering, leaving. It is not that a dark patch has appeared in the man's life; the darkness has become the medium he moves through.

## "And he for whom Allah has not appointed light, for him there is no light"

This closing sentence is the hinge of the whole passage. Ibn Kathir: one whom Allah does not guide is ignorant and doomed, "an utter loser and disbeliever." He sets it beside "Whomsoever Allah sends astray, none can guide him" (7:186), and then says that this is in contrast to what Allah says about the believers: "**Allah guides to His Light whom He wills**" (24:35).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same pairing: this sentence about the disbelievers is like the one that appeared earlier for the believers in ayah 35. It describes the deprivation of the disbelievers from the Nur of guidance, which they lost by denying the injunctions of Allah — and when they have lost *Allah's* Nur of guidance, how can they get any other light?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out a further implication, citing Mazhari: no one can become a perspicacious scholar merely by having the resource of insight and knowledge; rather, it is bestowed by the grace of Allah alone. It is for this reason that those regarded as naïve in worldly matters prove themselves very knowledgeable in the cognizance of the Hereafter, while many who are regarded as very intelligent and knowledgeable in worldly matters prove themselves completely ignorant in perceiving and comprehending it. Light is not the same thing as cleverness. One is given; the other is acquired and can be entirely misdirected.

Ibn Kathir ends his comment on these ayat not with an argument but with a duʿāʼ — a supplication, a prayer of asking: we ask Allah the Almighty to put light in our hearts, and give us light on our right and on our left, and to increase us in light.

## Living it

**Test your deeds against the two failures named in ayah 39.** Ibn Kathir specifies that deeds are found unaccepted either because of a lack of sincere belief, or because the person did not follow the proper ways of the Sharīʿah. So the two honest questions about any act of worship or service are: *For whom am I doing this?* and *Is this how Allah asked for it to be done?* A deed that fails either question can still look impressive from a distance — that is precisely the property of a mirage.

**Beware of the accounting you do for yourself.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's first category are people confident that, according to their own reckoning, their good acts will be rewarded. The disaster in the parable is not that they had no ledger; it is that theirs was not the ledger being read. And, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, they discover their blunder in the Hereafter, when it will be of no avail.

**Answer the two questions.** Where are you going, and where are the people you follow going? Ibn Kathir's account of the man who could answer neither is the warning of ayah 40 in miniature. Following is not itself the fault; following without knowing whom you follow or where it leads is.

**Ask for light, and keep asking.** Since ayah 40 states plainly that the one for whom Allah has not appointed light has no light, the only sane response is the one Ibn Kathir models: to ask Allah for light in the heart, light on every side, and more of it.

passages.title: Signs of Allah's dominion in creation
passages.tafsir:
This passage takes the eye that has just been trained on the private conduct of believers and lifts it outward — to the birds in the air, the clouds gathering overhead, the turning of night into day, and every creeping and walking thing on earth. The thread running through ayat 41–46 is a single claim: the whole universe is already worshipping its Master, already obeying, already displaying His power — and the only question left is whether *you* will see it. The passage opens twice with **"See you not…"** (ayah 41 and again ayah 43), and closes in ayah 46 with Allah having sent down manifest signs and guiding whom He wills. Sight is the theme; the sights are the evidence.

## Ayah 41 — a universe already at prayer

**"See you not that Allah, He it is Whom glorify whosoever is in the heavens and the earth, and the birds with wings outspread?"**

Ibn Kathir explains the sweep of this bluntly: *whosoever is in the heavens and on the earth* means the angels, mankind, the jinn, the animals — **and even inanimate objects**. All of them glorify Him. He supports this with the parallel ayah, *"The seven heavens and the earth and all that is therein, glorify Him"* (17:44).

Then the ayah zooms in on one image: **wa'l-ṭayru ṣāffāt** — "and the birds with wings outspread." Ibn Kathir's comment is worth sitting with: *while they are flying* they glorify their Lord and worship Him "with the glorification with which they are inspired and to which they are guided." The bird gliding overhead with its wings held out in a row is not on a break from worship. The flight *is* the worship.

### "Of each one He knows indeed his Salah and his glorification"

**kullun qad ʿalima ṣalātahu wa tasbīḥahu.** Ibn Kathir reads this as: He has guided every creature to its own way of worshipping Allah, may He be glorified. Every species has a liturgy suited to what it is.

This is the phrase the commentators dwell on, and the sources before us preserve **two genuine positions** among the scholars. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays them side by side. (Throughout, *tasbīḥ* is the Arabic word for glorifying Allah; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's rendering of the ayah puts it as "proclaiming Allah's purity.")

**First view — glorification by action.** Sufyan (رح) explains *tasbīḥ* here as follows: Allah has created everything in this universe — earth, heavens, sun, moon, stars, water, fire, air, sand — with a purpose, and they are all performing, all the time, the task they are assigned. **They cannot refuse to perform their assigned job.** This obedience and submission in carrying out the assigned job *is* the tasbīḥ referred to here. On this reading, "their Tasbih is by action and not by words": by their actions they are confirming that they perform this worship because they believe Allah Taʿālā to be Pure and Almighty.

**Second view — a real glorification we cannot hear.** Zamakhsharī and some other commentators, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports, have elaborated that it is "not improbable" that Allah has placed so much sense and understanding in everything that they do recognise their Creator and Master — and not improbable that He has taught them some sort of speech, and some special tasbīḥ and worship in which they keep themselves busy.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the closing words of the ayah — *everyone knows one's own way of praying and proclaiming Allah's purity* — contain an allusion in this second direction. What it indicates is that **all creatures are busy in tasbīḥ and worship of Allah, but the manner of worship of each creature is different**: angels worship in one way, human beings in another, trees and vegetation in another still, and rocks and minerals in yet another manner.

The supporting proof offered is Allah's word, **"He who gave everything its shape, then guidance"** (20:50) — that is, Allah created everything and then gave guidance to them. That guidance shows itself in two ways: everything is obeying Allah and performing its assigned duty diligently; and everything has been guided how to fulfil the need of its existence with such perfection that even the best of minds get boggled. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points to how creative and complicated are the nests and holes creatures make for their living, and how they strive and work hard to find and collect their food — in itself, it says, a great wonder.

**Neither view is presented as the settled one, and we should not settle it either.** What both agree on is the substance: nothing in creation is idle, and nothing in creation is silent before Allah.

### "And Allah is All-Aware of what they do"

Ibn Kathir: Allah tells us that He knows all of that, and **nothing at all is hidden from Him**. This is the quiet edge of the ayah. If He registers the worship of a bird in mid-air and a stone in the ground, then the human being — the one creature that *can* refuse its assigned task — is not slipping past Him unnoticed either.

## Ayah 42 — the ownership behind the worship

**"And to Allah belongs the sovereignty of the heavens and the earth, and to Allah is the return."**

Ayah 42 supplies the reason the whole universe worships: it is His. Ibn Kathir draws out the full weight of *mulk* (sovereignty): He is the Ruler and Controller, the One Who is worshipped and besides Whom none other is to be worshipped, and **there is none to put back His judgement**.

Then, *"and to Allah is the return"* — Ibn Kathir explains this as the Day of Resurrection, when He will judge as He wills, citing *"that He may requite those who do evil with that which they have done…"* (53:31). Ibn Kathir closes: He is the Creator and Sovereign, and His is indeed the Authority in this world and the next; to Him be praise at the beginning and in the end.

So ayat 41–42 form one movement: **everything glorifies Him** (41) **because everything belongs to Him, and everything returns to Him** (42).

## Ayat 43–44 — watching the weather as revelation

**"See you not that Allah drives the clouds gently, then joins them together, then makes them into a heap of layers, and you see the rain come forth from between them…"**

The second *"See you not"* begins the passage's most detailed sign, and Ibn Kathir walks through it stage by stage — because the ayah itself is staged.

- **yuzjī — "drives gently."** Ibn Kathir: Allah drives the clouds *from the beginning, when they are formed and are still weak*. This, he says, is the "gentle driving." The verb catches the cloud at its faintest, before there is anything to look at.
- **thumma yu'allifu baynahu — "then joins them together."** He brings them together **after they have been scattered**.
- **thumma yajʿaluhu rukāman — "then makes them into a heap of layers."** He piles them up on top of one another.
- **fa-tarā al-wadqa yakhruju min khilālihi.** *Al-wadq* means the rain; *min khilālihi* means **from the gaps between them**. Ibn Kathir notes this is how **Ibn ʿAbbās** and **Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk** understood it.

Notice how many separate acts stand between a scattered vapour and a drop of rain landing on your roof. The ayah does not simply say "Allah sends rain." It slows the process down so you can count the steps — and every verb has Allah as its subject.

### The four winds

Ibn Kathir reports that **ʿUbayd bin ʿUmayr Al-Laythī** said: "Allah sends the scatterer [wind], which stirs up that which is on the surface of the earth. Then he sends the generator [wind], which forms the clouds. Then He sends the joiner [wind] which brings them together. Then He sends the fertilizer [wind] which fertilizes or 'seeds' the clouds." Ibn Kathir notes this was **recorded by Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Jarir**. (This is the statement of an early authority, not a report from the Prophet ﷺ.)

### "Mountains of ice" — where the scholars differ

**"and He sends down from [min] the sky, from [min] mountains in it of [min] ice."** Three times the small preposition *min* appears, and the grammarians and mufassirūn discussed what each one is doing.

Ibn Kathir reports that **some of the grammarians** said: the first *min* describes the place from which it is coming, the second specifies from which part of the sky it comes, and the third means "some kind of mountains." This is based on the view of those scholars of tafsīr who take **"mountains" literally**: that there are mountains of hail in the sky, from which Allah sends down ice.

**As for those who say** that "mountains" here is used as a **metaphor for clouds**, Ibn Kathir notes, they think the second *min* is also used to describe the place from which the ice is coming, and is thus interchangeable with the first. Ibn Kathir ends the discussion with the scholar's honest formula: **"And Allah knows best."**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's own gloss lines up with that second reading: here the word *samāʼ* ("sky") is purported for clouds, and *jibāl* ("mountains") for big masses of clouds, while hail is called *barad*.

The lesson for a reader is as much about method as about meteorology: where the early scholars genuinely differed, the tafsīr records both and refuses to force a verdict.

### Mercy and punishment from the same sky

**"and strikes therewith whom He wills, and averts it from whom He wills."** Ibn Kathir offers two possible senses:

1. *"Strikes therewith"* may mean **with what He sends down from the sky of different kinds of rain and hail** — so *He strikes therewith whom He wills* means **by His mercy towards them**, and *averts it from whom He wills* means He withholds rain from them.
2. Or *"strikes therewith"* may mean **with hail, as a punishment** towards whomever He wills, striking their fruits and destroying their crops and trees — while He **averts it from whomever He wills as a mercy** towards them.

Either way, the same clouds you watch are an instrument of His will, distributing mercy here and withholding or afflicting there. Rain is never merely weather.

**"The vivid flash of its lightning nearly blinds the sight."** Ibn Kathir: the brightness of its lightning almost takes away their sight **if the eyes follow it and try to look at it**. A single flash, and the strongest human sense is overwhelmed.

### Ayah 44 — the turning of night and day

**yuqallibu Llāhu al-layla wa'n-nahār.** Ibn Kathir explains: He is controlling them, so that **He takes something from the length of one and adds it to the other**, which is short, until they become equal; then He does the opposite, so that the one which was short becomes long and vice versa. And Allah is the One Who is controlling that **by His command, power, might and knowledge**.

That is a sign no one can miss and almost no one notices, because it is delivered in daily instalments of a few minutes.

**"Truly, in this is indeed a lesson (ʿibrah) for those who have insight."** Ibn Kathir: this is an indication of His greatness, may He be exalted — and he places beside it, *"Verily, in the creation of the heavens and the earth, and in the alternation of night and day, there are indeed signs for men of understanding"* (3:190) and thereafter.

Here is something a reader may notice for himself in the Arabic of the two ayat, though the commentators before us do not spell it out: the same word, **al-abṣār**, sits at the end of both. The lightning nearly takes away *al-abṣār* — the sight of those who merely stare at it; and the lesson is for *ūlū'l-abṣār* — those possessed of sight, which Ibn Kathir's rendering gives as "those who have insight." The same faculty that is defeated by a flash is the faculty that, used properly, reads the whole sky as evidence. The difference is not in the eye but in what the heart does with what the eye receives.

## Ayah 45 — every moving creature from water

**"Allah has created every moving creature (dābbah) from water."**

Ibn Kathir frames this as Allah mentioning **His complete and almighty power**: to create all the different kinds of animals, with their various forms, colours, and ways of moving and stopping — **from one kind of water**. One raw material; endless outcomes.

The ayah then sorts them by how they move:

- **"Of them there are some that creep on their bellies"** — like snakes and so on;
- **"and some that walk on two legs"** — like humans and birds;
- **"and some that walk on four"** — like cattle and all kinds of animals.

**"Allah creates what He wills."** Ibn Kathir: meaning by His power, because **what He wills happens and what He does not will does not happen**. And so the ayah seals it: *"Verily, Allah is able to do all things."*

A closing reflection of my own, not something the two commentaries state: ayah 41 told us each creature knows its own way of praying, and ayah 45 shows those same creatures in their variety — the one on its belly, the one on two legs, the one on four. Read together, the differences in how creatures move sit alongside the differences in how they worship. But that pairing is the reader's, not the mufassirūn's, and it should be held lightly.

## Ayah 46 — the signs are manifest; the seeing is a gift

**"We have indeed sent down manifest Ayat. And Allah guides whom He wills to the Straight Path."**

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah states that in this Qur'an He has revealed **many clear and unambiguous rulings, words of wisdom and parables** — and that He guides **people of understanding, insight and intellect** to ponder them and understand them.

This is the passage's closing turn, and it is a humbling one. Ayah 41 and ayah 43 both asked, *"See you not?"* The clouds are there for everyone. The lightning flashes over the believer and the denier alike. The night shortens for the attentive and the heedless equally. Ayah 46 tells us why some people read all of that as evidence and others walk under it for a lifetime and see nothing: **"And Allah guides whom He wills to the Straight Path."** The signs are *mubayyināt* — manifest, made plain; the deficiency was never in the evidence.

## Living it

The passage does not end in an argument to win. It ends in a way of moving through the world.

**Take the "See you not" literally.** The passage's method is to send you outdoors. Watch a bird hold its wings out. Watch clouds that were scattered this morning pile up on top of one another by afternoon. Notice, this month, that the light is going a little earlier than last month. Ibn Kathir calls the alternation of night and day *an indication of His greatness*.

**Let creation shame you gently, not crush you.** On Sufyan's (رح) reading, everything around you is performing exactly the task it was assigned and **cannot refuse**. You are the exception — the one creature given the capacity to refuse. To join the tasbīḥ of the universe is simply to do, willingly, what everything else does by nature.

**Hold rain and drought both as His.** Ibn Kathir's two readings of *"strikes therewith whom He wills"* mean the believer never reads weather as luck. What arrives and what is withheld are equally decisions of the One to whom belongs the sovereignty of the heavens and the earth (ayah 42).

**Ask for the sight, not just the evidence.** Since ayah 46 makes guidance His to give, the fitting response to a sky full of signs is not self-congratulation for noticing but a request: that He make us among *ūlū'l-abṣār*, those who take the lesson, and guide us to the Straight Path.

passages.title: The hypocrites called to the Messenger's judgement
passages.tafsir:
These eight ayat put two communities side by side and let their behaviour do the talking. One group says "we believe and we obey" — until the ruling of Allah and His Messenger ﷺ threatens to go against them. The other group, when summoned to that same ruling, says only: *we hear and we obey*. What holds the passage together is a single test — **what a person does when the judgement of revelation runs against his own interest** — and the passage moves from exposing the failure (47–50), to portraying the success (51–52), to unmasking the noisy oaths that try to paper over the failure (53), and finally to setting out plainly where the Messenger's ﷺ responsibility ends and yours begins (54).

## The incident behind the passage

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports, on the authority of Tabari and others, that these ayat were revealed on a specific occasion. A hypocrite named Bishr had a dispute and a running enmity with a Jewish man over a piece of land. The Jewish man suggested that they take the case before the Prophet ﷺ for judgement. Bishr refused — because he knew well that he was in the wrong, and that if the dispute were taken to the Prophet ﷺ he would decide it on merit, and Bishr would lose. He asked instead that the matter be taken to Kaʿb ibn Ashraf.

Sit with the shape of that story. The man who *claimed* Islam was the one running from the Prophet's ﷺ court; the non-Muslim was the one willing to stand in it. Nothing exposes a hollow claim of faith more completely.

## "We believe" — and then a party turns away (47)

Ibn Kathir opens by saying that Allah is telling us the characteristics of the hypocrites: people **who show one thing while hiding another**. They say with their tongues, "We have believed in Allah and in the Messenger, and we obey" — and then a party of them turns away. Ibn Kathir's comment is blunt: *their actions contradict their deeds, and they say that which they do not do*. Allah's own verdict follows immediately — **"such are not believers."** The claim is on the tongue; the verdict is on the record.

## Being "called to Allah and His Messenger" (48)

What does it actually mean to be *called to Allah and His Messenger to judge between them*? Ibn Kathir explains: it means being asked **to follow the guidance which Allah has revealed to His Messenger ﷺ**. So this is not only about a courtroom. Any time revelation is placed before a person as the thing that settles the matter, he is being "called to Allah and His Messenger."

And the reason for turning away, says Ibn Kathir, is that **they are too arrogantly proud of themselves to follow him ﷺ**. He points to the parallel in Sūrah al-Nisāʼ, where Allah asks about those "who claim that they believe in that which has been sent down to you, and that which was sent down before you," and concludes: "you see the hypocrites turn away from you with aversion" (4:60–61). The same disease, diagnosed twice.

## مُذْعِنِينَ — coming eagerly, for the wrong reason (49)

Then comes the ayah that makes the whole diagnosis undeniable. **"But if the truth is on their side, they come to him willingly with submission"** — *mudhʿinīn* (مُذْعِنِينَ), which Ibn Kathir explains as meaning that if the ruling will be in their favour and not against them, then they will come, and will listen, and will obey.

Feel the sting in this. The same man who "refuses and turns away" in ayah 48 arrives *willingly* in ayah 49 — same court, same judge, same revelation. The only variable is the expected outcome. Ibn Kathir spells it out: but if the ruling will go against him, *he turns away and demands something that goes against the truth, and he prefers to refer for judgement to someone other than the Prophet ﷺ so that his false claims may prevail*. And then the line worth underlining:

> "His acceptance in the beginning was not because he believed that it was the truth, but because it happened to be in accordance with his desires. So when the truth went against what he was hoping for, he turned away from it." — Ibn Kathir

That is the definition of the disease. Such a person never submitted to revelation at all; revelation simply happened, on that occasion, to agree with him. His real judge, throughout, was his own desire — and it was never overruled.

## The three questions of ayah 50

Ayah 50 poses three possibilities in a row: **is there a disease in their hearts? or do they doubt? or do they fear that Allah and His Messenger will wrong them in judgement?**

Ibn Kathir treats these as exhausting the options: their situation *cannot be anything else* — they must necessarily have a disease in their hearts, or else they have some doubts about the religion, or they are afraid that Allah and His Messenger ﷺ will be unjust in their ruling against them. And then his verdict: **"Whichever it is, it is pure disbelief, and Allah knows which of these characteristics each one of them has."** The precise diagnosis in each individual case is left to Allah's knowledge; what is certain is that all three roads lead to the same place.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the rhetorical questions with a different emphasis, and the difference is instructive. Reading the ayah against the incident of Bishr, it takes the questions as *negating* firm infidelity or doubt about prophethood **as the real cause** of his evasion of the Prophet's ﷺ court. Hypocrites certainly do harbour disbelief and doubt — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān grants that this is "obvious and proven" — but that was not the underlying cause here. The driver was simpler and more humiliating: Bishr knew well that if the case were placed before the Prophet ﷺ he would lose it, because he would decide it on merit.

The two readings are not really at war. Ibn Kathir names the underlying condition; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names the immediate motive. Between them you get the whole picture: a diseased heart, moved on the day by nothing more elevated than the certainty of losing the case.

Then Allah closes the file: **"Nay, it is they themselves who are the wrongdoers."** Ibn Kathir: they are the evildoers who commit immoral actions, and **Allah and His Messenger ﷺ are innocent of the injustice and unfairness that they imagine** — exalted be Allah and His Messenger above such a thing. The suspicion they projected onto the judgement of Allah was in truth a portrait of themselves.

## "We hear and we obey" (51)

Having shown the counterfeit, Allah shows the genuine article. Ibn Kathir says that here Allah tells us the attributes of the believers who respond to Allah and His Messenger and **who seek no other way apart from the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger ﷺ**.

Notice how the ayah frames it: this is **"the only saying of the faithful believers"** when they are called to Allah and His Messenger to judge between them. And notice that the believers are not described as those who are *pleased* with every ruling, or who agree with it in advance. They are described by their sentence: **سَمِعْنَا وَأَطَعْنَا — "we hear and we obey."** Ibn Kathir explains the phrase as meaning *to hear in order to obey*: hearing that is already on its way to action, not hearing that will consider the matter later.

Then Allah names them *al-muflihūn*, the successful. Ibn Kathir defines that success concretely: **achieving what one wants and being saved from what one fears.** Both halves — the good attained and the dread removed.

### The Companions on "we hear and we obey"

Ibn Kathir gathers reports around this phrase. Qatadah related — "we were told" — that when **ʿUbādah ibn as-Sāmit**, who had been present at al-ʿAqabah and at Badr and was one of the leaders of the Ansar, was dying, he said to his nephew Junādah ibn Abī Umayyah: "Shall I not tell you what you must do and what is your due?" He said, "Yes." ʿUbādah said:

> "You have to listen and obey when times are easy and when they are hard, when you feel energetic and when you do not want to, and when you feel selfish. You have to train your tongue to speak the truth. Do not go against those who are in authority, unless they openly command you to commit acts of disobedience to Allah. Whenever you are commanded to do something that goes against the Book of Allah, then follow the Book of Allah."

A dying man's last counsel, and every clause is aimed at exactly the weakness ayat 47–49 exposed: obedience that survives hardship, reluctance and self-interest — and a clear limit, that no created authority is obeyed in disobedience to Allah.

Qatadah also related that **Abū ad-Dardāʼ** said: "There is no Islam except through obedience to Allah, and no goodness except in Jamāʿah. Sincerity is to Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, and to the Khalīfah and all the believers." And that **ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb** (may Allah be pleased with him) used to say: "The bonds of Islam are *lā ilāha illallāh*, establishing prayer, paying Zakāh and obeying those whom Allah has given authority over the affairs of the Muslims." Ibn Kathir notes these were recorded by Ibn Abī Hātim, and adds that the reports stating the obligation of obeying the Book of Allah, the Sunnah of His Messenger, the Rightly-Guided Khalīfahs and the Imams *when they command us to obey Allah* are far too many to quote.

## The four conditions of ayah 52

Ayah 52 sets out what Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls **four conditions for success and victory**: obey Allah, obey His Messenger ﷺ, have awe of Allah, and observe *taqwā* of Him. Those who bind themselves to these four, it says, are the ones who are successful and victorious in this world and the Hereafter.

Ibn Kathir unpacks each. "Whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger" — *in what he is commanded with, and avoids what he is forbidden*. "And fears Allah" — this looks **backward, to his past sins**. "And has taqwā of Him" — this looks **forward, regarding sins he may commit in the future**. So the believer's inner life is guarded at both ends of time: fear over what he has already done, watchfulness over what he might yet do. (Ibn Kathir's gloss is itself the plainest definition of the term *taqwā* here: guarding oneself against sins one may yet commit.)

Their reward is *al-fāʼizūn* — rendered by Ibn Kathir as "the successful" and by Maʿārif ul Qurʼān as "the victorious." Ibn Kathir explains: **those who will attain all goodness and be saved from all evil in this world and the Hereafter.**

### The Roman villager and Sayyidnā ʿUmar

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates, from Tafsīr Qurtubī, an incident that shows how much is folded into this one ayah. Sayyidnā ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) was standing in the Prophet's mosque when a Roman villager appeared beside him and declared the *shahādah*. ʿUmar asked what the matter was. The man said he had accepted Islam for Allah's sake. Asked whether there was a particular reason, he said yes: he had read the Torah, the Injīl, the Zabūr and a number of other books brought by past messengers — and then he heard a verse of the Qurʼān recited by a Muslim prisoner and realised that in that small verse all the older books had been condensed. That convinced him it was Allah's revelation. The verse was this one, 24:52.

He then offered his own commentary on it: *"whoever obeys Allah"* relates to the obligations owed to Allah; *"and His Messenger"* refers to the Prophet's ﷺ traditions; *"and fears Allah"* alludes to one's past life; *"and observes taqwā of Him"* is for the remaining life. Whoever acts upon these four is given the glad tiding that such are *al-fāʼizūn* — and, he said, the *fāʼiz* is the one who gets deliverance from Jahannam and earns a place in Paradise.

Hearing this, ʿUmar said its endorsement is found in the saying of the Prophet ﷺ that Allah had graced him with *jawāmiʿ al-kalim* — comprehensive expressions in which the words are few but the meanings are vast. (Reported in Tafsīr Qurtubī, as cited by Maʿārif ul Qurʼān.)

## "Do not swear" (53)

Ayah 53 turns to a different tactic of the same people. Ibn Kathir explains that this concerns the hypocrites who had promised the Messenger ﷺ and sworn that if he were to command them to go out for battle, they would go. They swore by Allah their strongest oaths.

Allah's reply is startling in its brevity: **"Say: swear not."** Ibn Kathir: *do not swear this oath.* Then, **"obedience is known"** — of which Ibn Kathir reports the interpretation that *your obedience is known*, that is, it is known to be **merely verbal and not accompanied by action**; every time you swear an oath, you lie.

He shows this is a settled pattern in the Qurʼān's portrait of hypocrisy: "They swear to you that you may be pleased with them" (9:96); "They have made their oaths a screen for their evil actions" (58:16). Oaths used not as truth-telling but as *cover*. And Ibn Kathir adds that lying is part of their nature even in matters they choose for themselves, citing Sūrah al-Hashr: they promise their disbelieving allies among the People of the Scripture that if they are expelled they will go out with them, and if they are attacked they will help them — "But Allah is Witness that they verily are liars" — and in the event they neither go out, nor help, nor prevail (59:11–12).

The practical lesson lands hard: **loud swearing is not a substitute for a single act of obedience.** Where the deed is absent, intensifying the oath only sharpens the exposure.

## Where responsibility divides (54)

The passage closes with a command and a clean division of accounts. **"Say: Obey Allah and obey the Messenger"** — which Ibn Kathir explains as: *follow the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger ﷺ*.

Then: "but if you turn away" — that is, says Ibn Kathir, if you ignore what he has brought to you — **"he is only responsible for the duty placed on him"**: conveying the Message and fulfilling the trust. **"And you for that placed on you"**: accepting it, venerating it, and doing as it commanded. Two burdens, two ledgers. The Messenger ﷺ discharged his the moment he delivered the message clearly. Yours is not discharged until you act.

**"If you obey him, you shall be on the right guidance"** — and Ibn Kathir gives the reason: *because he calls to the straight path*, the path of Allah "to Whom belongs all that is in the heavens and all that is in the earth" (42:53). Guidance is not a reward arbitrarily attached to obedience; obedience to him ﷺ simply *is* walking that road.

And the final clause, **"The Messenger's duty is only to convey in a clear way,"** Ibn Kathir places alongside "your duty is only to convey and on Us is the reckoning" (13:40) and "So remind them — you are only one who reminds. You are not a dictator over them" (88:21–22). The Prophet ﷺ was never charged with forcing hearts open. He conveys with clarity; the response, and the reckoning for it, belong to Allah.

## Living it

The passage leaves an honest reader with one question, and it is not a question about seventh-century Madinah. **When the ruling of Allah and His Messenger ﷺ goes against what I want — my money, my family dispute, my reputation, my preferred opinion — do I still come?**

By the standard of these ayat, agreeing with revelation when it happens to suit me proves nothing at all. Ibn Kathir has already ruled on that case: such acceptance "was not because he believed that it was the truth, but because it happened to be in accordance with his desires." Faith becomes visible precisely at the point where the ruling costs something. The believers of ayah 51 are not people without preferences; they are people whose preferences do not get a vote once the matter is settled by the Book and the Sunnah. Their whole answer is two words — *we hear and we obey* — and Allah calls them the successful for it.

passages.title: The promise of succession, security, and worship
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat are Allah's promise to the believing community that He will settle them in the earth, establish the religion He has chosen for them, and exchange their fear for security — followed immediately by what that promise demands. Ayah 55 is the promise and its condition; ayah 56 is the daily discipline that keeps a community inside the promise; ayah 57 removes the last excuse for fear by telling the Prophet ﷺ that the people frightening him cannot escape Allah at all.

## The moment it was revealed

Ibn Kathir records that Ar-Rabiʿ bin Anas narrated from Abu al-ʿĀliyah that the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions spent nearly ten years in Makkah calling people in secret to worship Allah alone with no partner or associate. They lived in a state of fear, and were not instructed to fight until after they were commanded to migrate to Madinah. And even in Madinah, Abu al-ʿĀliyah says, "they were afraid and they carried their weapons morning and evening" — for as long as Allah willed. Then Allah revealed this ayah.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports a separate narration: Qurtubi, on the authority of Abul ʿAliyah, relates that even after the migration to Madinah the danger of attack never let up. So someone asked him ﷺ: *would a time come when we would be able to live in peace without wearing our weaponry?* He ﷺ replied, "Yes, the time is coming very soon." On that occasion these verses were revealed. (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sources this to Qurtubi and Baḥr.)

Al-Barāʾ bin ʿĀzib, may Allah be pleased with him, said simply: "This Ayah was revealed when we were in a state of extreme fear."

Read ayah 55 in that voice. It is not a triumphal announcement from a position of strength; it is a promise made to an exhausted, outnumbered, armed-and-watchful community. Ibn Kathir notes that this ayah is like the ayah *"And remember when you were few and were reckoned weak in the land"* (8:26).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a further dimension from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him (in *Baḥr Muḥīṭ*): these verses relate a promise Allah made concerning the Ummah of Muhammad ﷺ before their creation, in the Torah and the Injīl.

## Three promises in one sentence

Ayah 55 contains three distinct guarantees, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān counts them exactly so: that his Ummah will be made vicegerent on earth and will rule over it; that the religion Allah has favoured for them, Islam, will be made victorious; and that they will be given such power and grandeur that they will have no fear of anyone.

The English translation Ibn Kathir's commentary works from is emphatic at every step — "He will **certainly** grant them succession in the land… He **will** grant them the authority… He will **surely** give them in exchange a safe security after their fear."

**Succession.** Ibn Kathir explains what granting succession means: they would become "the leaders and rulers of mankind, through whom He would reform the world and to whom people would submit."

**Establishment.** The second promise is that Allah "will grant them the authority to practise their religion which He has chosen for them."

**Exchange.** The third is the most tender: *He will surely give them in exchange a safe security after their fear.* The wording is one of exchange, not merely reduction. For men who carried weapons morning and evening, this was the very thing they had asked for.

## "As He granted it to those before them"

Ayah 55 anchors the promise in precedent: *as He granted it to those before them.* Ibn Kathir connects this to Mūsā's words to his people, *"It may be that your Lord will destroy your enemy and make you successors on the earth"* (7:129), and to *"And We wished to do a favour to those who were weak in the land"* (28:5). This is how Allah has dealt before with a believing community that was oppressed and held on.

## The condition, stated plainly

The promise is not unconditional, and the ayah is careful about this at both ends. At the start: *"those among you who believe and do righteous good deeds."* At the close: *"if they worship Me and do not associate anything with Me."*

On these closing words Ibn Kathir brings the narration that Imam Ahmad recorded from Anas, that Muʿādh bin Jabal, may Allah be pleased with him, told him — a narration also recorded in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs. Muʿādh was riding behind the Prophet ﷺ on a donkey. Three times the Prophet ﷺ called him by name, and three times Muʿādh answered, "Here I am at your service, O Messenger of Allah," before the question came:

> "Do you know the rights that Allah has over His servants?" I said, "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said, "The rights that Allah has over His servants are that they should worship Him and not associate anything with Him."

Then the second half:

> "Do you know the rights that people have over Allah if they do that?" I said, "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said, "The rights that people have over Allah is that He will not punish them."

The content maps precisely onto ayah 55: worship Him alone, associate nothing with Him.

## How the promise was kept

Ibn Kathir shows that the Companions who heard this verse in fear lived to see it fulfilled. "This is what Allah did indeed do," he writes, "may He be glorified and exalted."

In the Prophet's ﷺ own lifetime: victory over Makkah, Khaybar, Bahrayn, all of the Arabian Peninsula and Yemen; jizyah taken from the Zoroastrians of Hajar and from some of the border lands of Syria; gifts exchanged with Heraclius the ruler of Byzantium, with the Muqawqis the ruler of Egypt and Alexandria, with the kings of Oman, and with An-Najāshī of Abyssinia who had become king after Aṣḥamah, may Allah have mercy on him.

Then Abu Bakr aṣ-Ṣiddīq, may Allah be pleased with him, "took over the reins of power and united the Ummah, preventing its disintegration" — taking control of the entire Peninsula and sending armies out: Khālid bin al-Walīd towards Persia, Abū ʿUbaydah and the commanders after him towards Syria, ʿAmr bin al-ʿĀṣ towards Egypt. Buṣrā, Damascus and the land of Ḥawrān were opened.

The people of Islam were then blessed that aṣ-Ṣiddīq was inspired to appoint ʿUmar al-Fārūq as his successor. Of him Ibn Kathir writes that "after the Prophets, the world never saw anyone like ʿUmar in excellence of conduct and perfect justice." In his time the rest of Syria, Egypt and most of Persia were conquered; Kisrā was defeated and retreated to the furthest point of his kingdom, and Caesar was brought low and withdrew to Constantinople. Under ʿUthmān, may Allah be pleased with him, the domains spread east and west — as far west as Cyprus, Andalusia, Kairouan and Sebta which adjoins the Atlantic, and as far east as China, with Iraq, Khurāsān and al-Ahwāz conquered. Ibn Kathir attributes this to a spiritual cause: "This was a blessing brought by his recitation and study of the Qurʼan, and his bringing the Ummah together to preserve and protect it."

And Ibn Kathir cites, as recorded *in the Ṣaḥīḥ*, the Prophet's ﷺ words: **"Allah showed me the earth and I looked at the east and the west. The dominion of my Ummah will reach everywhere I was shown."** He then adds: "And now we are enjoying that which Allah and His Messenger ﷺ promised us, for Allah and His Messenger ﷺ spoke the truth."

He also records what the Prophet ﷺ said to ʿAdiyy bin Ḥātim when he came in a delegation. "Do you know al-Ḥīrah?" ʿAdiyy said he did not know it but had heard of it. The Prophet ﷺ swore by the One in Whose Hand is his soul that Allah would make this matter prevail until a woman riding a camel would come from al-Ḥīrah and perform ṭawāf around the House without needing the protection of anybody, and the treasures of Kisrā the son of Hurmuz would be opened — and that wealth would be given out until there would be no one who would accept it. Later ʿAdiyy said: it is now happening that a woman travels from al-Ḥīrah and makes ṭawāf needing no one's protection, and I was among those who opened the treasure of Kisrā the son of Hurmuz — and by the One in Whose Hand is my soul, the third thing will also come to pass, because the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said it. (Ibn Kathir relates this without naming a collection.)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes: this passage is itself a proof of the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ, "because the forecast he had made came true exactly in the manner he had predicted."

## When the promise seemed to recede

The narration Ibn Kathir records does not stop at the victory. Allah caused His Prophet ﷺ to prevail over the Arabian Peninsula, and they felt safe and put down their weapons. Then Allah took His Prophet ﷺ, and they remained safe throughout the time of Abu Bakr, ʿUmar and ʿUthmān — "until what happened happened, and fear again prevailed over them, so they instituted a police force and guards." Then: **"They changed, so their situation changed."** One of the Salaf said, "The Khilāfah of Abu Bakr and ʿUmar was true and adhered to the Book of Allah" — and then recited this ayah.

Ibn Kathir applies the same principle: the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, were "the most committed of people after the Prophet ﷺ to the commands of Allah and the most obedient to Allah. Their victories were in accordance with their level of commitment." When the people afterwards fell short in their commitment to some of the commandments, "their strength and victory fell short accordingly."

That is the governing law of the ayah: the promise never failed; the condition was let go of. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same — this promise "is related to rectitude and firmness of faith, the righteous deeds and total obedience, and any difference in their degree will naturally make difference in the power and control of authority" — and observes that fourteen hundred years of Islamic history bear witness that wherever there was a just and righteous ruler, "he has received his share from this promise of Allah based on the extent of righteous deeds he has performed."

But the failure is never total. Ibn Kathir cites, as confirmed through more than one route in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs, the Prophet's ﷺ words: **"There will remain a group of my Ummah adhering to the truth, and those who forsake them or oppose them will not harm them until the Day of Resurrection."** Other reports run "…until the command of Allah comes to pass and they are like that," "…until they fight the Dajjāl," and "…until ʿĪsā bin Maryam comes down and they are prevailing." Ibn Kathir states that all of these reports are Ṣaḥīḥ and there is no contradiction between them.

## "But whoever disbelieved after this"

Ayah 55 ends with a warning: *"whoever disbelieved after this, they are the rebellious."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up the word *kufr* here. Its literal meaning is **thanklessness**; in conventional usage it is the opposite of faith. Both readings have room here: when Allah fulfils His promise and bestows power, authority, peace and stability on the Muslims, and someone then turns apostate, or avoids obeying the rules of the Islamic order — such a person is a transgressor on both counts. "Kufr and ingratitude are great sins in any situation, but after the establishment of Islamic rule, authority and grandeur the intensity of these sins is doubled." That, it says, is exactly why the ayah emphasises *baʿda dhālika* — **after that**. Ibn Kathir reads the phrase in the same direction: whoever then stops obeying Allah after that "has stopped obeying the command of his Lord, and that is a great sin."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports from Imam al-Baghawī that the scholars of tafsir explained that this Qurʼanic sentence came true for the first time upon those who assassinated the ruling caliph ʿUthmān, may Allah be pleased with him: the graces mentioned in the ayah were reduced, and they were afflicted with fear because of mutual killing — men who had been like brothers to one another. Baghawī relates the address ʿAbdullāh bin Salām, may Allah be pleased with him, gave during the commotion against ʿUthmān — that the angels of Allah had cordoned Madinah for security ever since the Prophet ﷺ came there, and that if ʿUthmān were assassinated they would go back and never return; and that Allah's sword had been in its sheath until then, and if it came out it would never go back in. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān comments that the sequence of internal bloodshed which began with the martyrdom of ʿUthmān has continued in the Ummah ever since, and that the great sacrifice of Ḥusayn bin ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with them both, happened within the same sequence.

## The passage and the Rightly Guided Caliphs

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān argues that this verse is a proof of the approval and esteem, in the sight of Allah, of the four Rightly Guided Caliphs. Its reasoning: the promise Allah made to His Messenger and his Ummah was completely fulfilled during the lifetime of those four Companions, so refusing to regard the earlier caliphates as legitimate — as some Rawāfiḍ do — would mean the Qurʼanic promise has still not been fulfilled. It rejects as untenable the alternative claim that the promise awaits the time of the Mahdī, since that would amount to saying the Ummah lived in disgrace and misery for a full fourteen hundred years. The conditions of faith and righteous deeds on which the promise was made, it says, were present in those Companions in perfection and totality.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also mentions a hadith, without naming a collection, that the caliphate would last thirty years after the Prophet ﷺ — understanding "caliphate" here as the Rightly Guided Caliphate, run exactly on his footsteps, which lasted to the time of ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him.

It further notes that at this point Ibn Kathir reports a hadith from Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Jābir bin Samurah, may Allah be pleased with him, that he heard the Prophet ﷺ say his Ummah would continue ruling until the twelve caliphs had passed. Ibn Kathir's comment is that these twelve upright caliphs will certainly appear, but not necessarily one after another with no gap — the four Rightly Guided Caliphs came consecutively, then ʿUmar bin ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz after an interval, and others at intervals after him. They are not necessarily all of the same status, nor are their times necessarily times of complete peace and tranquillity.

## Ayah 56: what keeps a community inside the promise

After all that history, the instruction is startlingly ordinary: *"And perform the Salah, and give the Zakah and obey the Messenger, that you may receive mercy."*

Ibn Kathir unpacks each. **Prayer** is glossed as "worshipping Allah Alone with no partner or associate" — the vertical relationship, which is precisely the condition stated in ayah 55. **Zakāh** he describes as "an act of kindness towards His poor and weak creatures" — the horizontal one. **Obeying the Messenger ﷺ** means "to do as he commands them and to avoid what he forbids them."

And the purpose clause: *that you may receive mercy.* Ibn Kathir is emphatic that this is no mere possibility — "No doubt, whoever does that, Allah will have mercy on him" — citing *"Allah will have His mercy on them"* (9:71).

A believer reading ayah 55 might ask what he can personally do about the succession of nations. Ayah 56 answers: pray, give, obey.

## Ayah 57: the enemy cannot escape

*"Consider not that the disbelievers can escape in the land. Their abode shall be the Fire — and worst indeed is that destination."*

Ibn Kathir reads *lā taḥsabanna* as addressed directly to the Prophet ﷺ: "do not think, O Muhammad." "Those who disbelieved" means "those who opposed and denied you." And *muʿjizīna fī al-arḍ* — that they can escape in the land — means, he says, "that they can flee from Allah.
