No, Allah is able to deal with them and He will punish them most severely for that." *Their abode* means in the Hereafter; and of the Fire he writes, "how terrible the consequences will be for the disbelievers, how evil a place to stay in and how awful a place to rest!"

A community waiting on a promise is tempted to overestimate those obstructing it. Ayah 57 shrinks them: they are not outside Allah's reach for a moment, and their final lodging is already known.

## Living it

**Do not measure the promise by the moment you are standing in.** It was revealed, as al-Barāʾ said, to people in a state of extreme fear who carried their weapons morning and evening.

**Watch the condition, not the outcome.** "They changed, so their situation changed." The ayah ties the promise to faith, righteous deeds, obedience and pure worship — so when a community weakens, the audit begins there.

**Then do the three small things.** Prayer that is really worship of Allah alone; zakāh as genuine kindness to the poor and weak; obedience to the Messenger ﷺ. Ayah 56 attaches mercy to those three, and Ibn Kathir says there is no doubt about it.

passages.title: Relaxed rules within the household: permission, dress, and shared meals
passages.tafsir:
Having taught the believers how strangers should approach a home, Allah now teaches how the people *inside* a home should treat one another. One balance holds them together: privacy is protected at the few moments it is genuinely at risk, and everywhere else household life is deliberately made easy.

## Two kinds of "asking permission"

Ibn Kathir points out the hinge: what was mentioned **earlier in the surah** had to do with how **unrelated people** should seek permission to enter upon one another; these ayat are about **people who are closely related** seeking permission to enter upon each other.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points back to verses 27, 28 and 29 of this surah under the heading of "seeking permission." Those verses bind the *visitor* — anyone arriving at a house must seek permission first, and that is obligatory. These verses address a different kind of *istiʼdhān*: people who **live together in the same house** and move freely from room to room, including the mahrams, the male relatives before whom a woman is not required to observe hijab. Even they should make their presence felt: clear the throat, let footsteps be heard. This kind of asking is preferable rather than obligatory, though to drop it altogether is *makrūh tanzīhī* — disliked as a matter of refinement rather than forbidden. It quotes Tafsir Mazhari: a man who intends to enter his own house while his mahram women are in it should not walk in unannounced, because one of them might be without clothes.

## The three ʿawrāt of the day (ayah 58)

Ayah 58 names three moments and gives them a title: **ثَلَاثُ عَوْرَاتٍ لَّكُمْ** — "(These) three (times) are of privacy for you."

Ibn Kathir explains each:

- **Before the Fajr prayer** — "because people are asleep in their beds at that time."
- **When you put off your clothes during the afternoon** (*wa ḥīna taḍaʿūna thiyābakum mina al-ẓahīrah*) — "at the time of rest, because a man may be in a state of undress with his wife at that time."
- **After the ʿIshāʼ prayer** — "because this is the time for sleep."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds what is at stake: to be walked in upon then, even by a very young but sensible child or a woman of the household, is deeply embarrassing, and at the very least it disturbs one's rest.

Who must knock? Those the ayah calls **مَا مَلَكَتْ أَيْمَانُكُمْ**, those your right hands possess, and children who have not yet reached puberty. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the phrase covers male and female slaves both, but adult male slaves fall under the category of non-mahrams in Islamic law, and a woman who owns one is obligated to observe hijab before him; so what is meant here are the slave girls and minor slaves who move about the house freely.

*Laysa ʿalaykum wa lā ʿalayhim junāḥun baʿdahunna* — "other than these times there is no sin on you or on them." Ibn Kathir: if they enter at another hour, there is no sin on you for letting them in, and no sin on them if they see something. They have been given permission to enter suddenly because they are the ones who go around in the house — to serve you and so on — and as such they may be forgiven things that others will not be forgiven. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the reason: at all other times people are busy with their normal duties and properly dressed, and those are not the usual times for intimacy.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, quoting Bayān ul-Qurʼān, notes that *junāḥ* is generally used for *sin* but is sometimes used for *harm* or *obstacle*, and it is that second sense here — so any doubt about children sinning is removed. Why address a command to children at all? Because the duty in fact falls on the adult men and women, who must explain to the young ones not to enter private rooms at these times without permission — in the same manner as a hadith instructs that children be taught prayer at seven and persuaded to offer it, and at ten be held firmly to it.

## "It has not been abrogated" — a lament from Ibn ʿAbbās

Ibn Kathir observes that although this ayah is quite clear and has not been abrogated, people hardly follow it — and ʿAbdullāh bin ʿAbbās denounced them for that. **Abu Dawud** recorded that Ibn ʿAbbās said: "Most of the people do not follow it, the ayah that speaks about asking permission, but I tell my servant woman to seek permission to enter." Abu Dawud added that ʿAṭāʼ likewise narrated that Ibn ʿAbbās commanded this. Ath-Thawrī narrated that Mūsā bin Abī ʿĀʼishah said, "I asked Ash-Shaʿbī about the ayah"; Ash-Shaʿbī said, "It has not been abrogated." Mūsā said, "But the people do not do that." Ash-Shaʿbī answered: **"May Allah help them."**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a report from Ibn Abī Ḥātim, as reported by Ibn Kathir: Ibn ʿAbbās said there are three verses people have stopped following — this verse of *istiʼdhān*; the verse on handing a share to relatives who are present at the division of an inheritance but have no claim on it, to console them (4:8); and the verse declaring that the noblest of you in the sight of Allah is the most mindful of Him, while in practice those regarded as honourable are whoever owns plenty of wealth and palatial houses. According to another narration he said Shayṭān has overpowered the people in respect of these three, and then said: "I have restrained even my slave girl not to come to me without permission at these three times."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports, again from Ibn Abī Ḥātim, that ʿIkrimah said two men asked Ibn ʿAbbās about this permission-seeking among near relatives. He replied: *inna Allāha sittīrun yuḥibbu al-sitr* — Allah keeps cover on many things, and He likes the same for others. When the verse came down, society was very simple: people used no curtains at the door, nor did they have large curtained beds, so a child or servant might come in unannounced at the worst moment. Now that people have both, that is considered enough for the purpose. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that Ibn Kathir, having reproduced this narration, said its chain of narrators to Ibn ʿAbbās is *ṣaḥīḥ* — authentic. From it, one thing is clear: where there is no apprehension of anyone seeing another uncovered or with his wife, some concession is allowed.

**How the jurists weighed it.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records difference among the scholars over whether this *istiʼdhān* is obligatory or merely commendable, and whether it still stands or was abrogated. The majority of jurists have ruled that the verse is firm and not abrogated, and the injunction obligatory for men and women alike (attributed to Qurtubi). Its own reading follows the reason behind the rule: where people habitually keep their concealable parts covered even at those hours and are careful to be intimate only when no one could walk in, it is no longer obligatory to restrain relatives and children — while remaining a desirable and commendable act.

## Ayah 59: when the child grows up

Ayah 59 closes the childhood exemption. **وَإِذَا بَلَغَ الْأَطْفَالُ مِنكُمُ الْحُلُمَ** — when the children among you reach *al-ḥulum*, puberty, let them seek permission as those senior to them in age do. Ibn Kathir: the children who used to seek permission only at the three times of privacy must now seek permission **at all times** — that is, with regard to those who are non-relatives, and at times when a man may be in a state of intimacy with his wife, even if it is not one of the three times stated above.

## Ayah 60: the elderly woman and the outer garment

Ayah 60 relaxes a rule from the other direction. **الْقَوَاعِدُ مِنَ النِّسَاءِ** — the *qawāʿid*. Ibn Kathir reports from Saʿīd bin Jubayr, Muqātil bin Ḥayyān, Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk and Qatādah that these are the women who no longer think that they can bear children; and *allātī lā yarjūna nikāḥan*, "who do not hope for marriage," means they no longer have any desire for marriage.

For such a woman there is no sin in **discarding her ثِيَاب**. Ibn Masʿūd said of it: "The *jilbāb* or *ridāʼ*," the outer wrap thrown over the ordinary clothes. Ibn Kathir reports that a similar view was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn ʿUmar, Mujāhid, Saʿīd bin Jubayr, Abu Ash-Shaʿthāʼ, Ibrāhīm An-Nakhaʿī, Al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, Az-Zuhrī, Al-Awzāʿī and others. Such women, as Ibn Kathir puts it, "do not have to cover themselves in the same way that other women have to." He also records that Abu Dawud reported Ibn ʿAbbās saying that the ayah "And tell the believing women to lower their gaze" (24:31) was abrogated and an exception made in the case of the *qawāʿid* who do not hope for marriage.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān counts this the **third** exemption in the surah's hijab passages. This exemption rests on a woman's own circumstance: if she has grown so old that no one would have any desire towards her and she is not marriageable, then in this respect non-mahrams are treated for her like mahrams.

**غَيْرَ مُتَبَرِّجَاتٍ بِزِينَةٍ** — "in such a way as not to show their adornment." Saʿīd bin Jubayr said: "They should not make a wanton display of themselves by removing their outer garment so that their adornment may be seen." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that the concession is granted on the condition that they do so without applying any makeup or adornment: it is for ease, not exhibition. Then **وَأَن يَسْتَعْفِفْنَ خَيْرٌ لَّهُنَّ** — "but to refrain is better for them." Ibn Kathir: not removing the outer garment, even though that is permissible for them, is better for them; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads it as better still that they avoid going before non-mahrams altogether — a thing can be permitted and the higher road still be to leave it. The ayah seals it with **وَاللَّهُ سَمِيعٌ عَلِيمٌ** — Allah is All-Hearer, All-Knower.

## Ayah 61: scruples that had become a burden

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene: these were people trained by the Qurʼan and by the company of the Prophet ﷺ to take the rights of people (*ḥuqūq al-ʿibād*) with the utmost seriousness, and their scruples had begun to tie them in knots. Several incidents are reported as the occasion of revelation; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān holds there is no contradiction between them, and that all of them together form its background.

**Embarrassment around disability.** Ibn Kathir reports that people felt too embarrassed to eat with the blind, because they could not see the food or where the best morsels were; with the lame, because they could not sit comfortably and their companions might take advantage of them; and with the sick, because they might not eat as much as others. Fearing they would be unfair to them in some way, they avoided the shared meal — and this, Ibn Kathir says, was the view of Saʿīd bin Jubayr and Miqsam. Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk gave a different picture: before the Prophet's mission people felt too embarrassed and too proud to eat with such people, lest they have to help them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Imam Baghawi from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, shows the same anxiety from the other side: companions who had these disabilities held back from eating with others for fear of causing them trouble. ʿAbdur-Razzāq recorded that Mujāhid said a man would take a blind, lame or sick person to the house of his brother, sister or aunt, and those disabled people would feel ashamed and say, "They are taking us to other people's houses."

**The keys.** Az-Zuhrī narrated from ʿUrwah that ʿĀʼishah said: the Muslims used to go out on military campaigns with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and would give their keys to people they trusted, saying, "We permit you to eat whatever you need" — but those trustees would say, "It is not permissible for us to eat; they have given us permission reluctantly and we are only trustees." Then Allah revealed **أَوْ مَا مَلَكْتُم مَّفَاتِحَهُ**, "or that whereof you hold keys." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the same account from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab, and notes that Musnad al-Bazzār also reported it on ʿĀʼishah's authority. It also cites Baghawi from Ibn ʿAbbās (among narrations it traces to Tafsir Mazhari) that *aw ṣadīqikum*, "or your friend," refers to the incident of Ḥārith bin ʿAmr, who went out for jihad with the Prophet ﷺ leaving his house in the care of his friend Mālik ibn Zayd, and returned to find him grown very weak — Mālik said he had not felt it right to eat anything from his house.

**A verse read too strictly.** ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that when Allah revealed *"O you who believe! Eat not up your property among yourselves unjustly"* (4:29), the Muslims said: Allah has forbidden us to consume one another's property unjustly, and food is the best of property, so it is not permissible for any of us to eat at anyone else's house — and the people stopped doing so. Then this ayah was revealed.

## Reading the list

The ayah lifts the *ḥaraj* — the restriction — from the blind, the lame, the sick, "nor on yourselves," then names your own houses, those of fathers, mothers, brothers, sisters, uncles and aunts, what you hold the keys to, and your friend's. Ibn Kathir makes two observations. First, "if you eat from your houses" is stated although it is obvious — it is the *starting point*, so that from it the houses of others may be mentioned. Sons' houses are included though not mentioned by name, and this is used as evidence by those who regard a son's wealth as being like the father's, citing the report — in the Musnad and the Sunan, through several routes — that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "You and your wealth belong to your father." Second, on "that whereof you hold the keys," Saʿīd bin Jubayr and As-Suddī said this refers to a people's servants, whether a slave or otherwise: there is nothing wrong with their eating from the food that is stored with them, within reason. Of the friend's house Ibn Kathir adds the governing condition: there is no sin on you in eating from their houses, **so long as you know that this does not upset them and they do not dislike it**.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān turns that condition into a ruling. The permission rests on a custom: among the Arabs it was normal to eat freely in the houses of close relatives with no formality, and they would even bring poor, sick or needy people to eat at another's house. So wherever that custom is not in vogue, or the owner's consent is doubtful, eating without permission is **forbidden** — and in our own time no one would like even a close relative to eat in his house unasked, so the permission does not apply unless a person is absolutely sure his eating there would cause no problem or displeasure. By the same logic the concession is **not restricted** to the relatives named in the verse — it extends to others, on that same condition of certainty (attributed to Mazhari). And it is not right to say the ruling belonged to the early days of Islam and was later abrogated: it has been in force from the beginning and always will be; what varies is whether its condition — certainty of the owner's permission — is met (attributed to Mazhari).

## Together or apart

**لَيْسَ عَلَيْكُمْ جُنَاحٌ أَن تَأْكُلُوا جَمِيعًا أَوْ أَشْتَاتًا** — no sin on you whether you eat together or apart. Ibn ʿAbbās mentions that a man would feel embarrassed and refrain from eating alone until someone else came along, and Allah made the matter easier for them. Qatādah identifies a clan of Banū Kinānah who during the Jāhiliyyah held eating alone to be a source of shame.

Yet Ibn Kathir notes that eating with others is more blessed and is better:

- **Imam Ahmad** recorded from Waḥshī bin Ḥarb, from his father, from his grandfather, that a man said to the Prophet ﷺ, "We eat but we do not feel satisfied." He said: *"Perhaps you are eating separately. Eat together and mention the Name of Allah, and He will bless the food for you."* Ibn Kathir notes it was also recorded by **Abu Dawud** and **Ibn Majah**.
- **Ibn Majah** also recorded that Sālim reported from his father, from ʿUmar, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"Eat together and not separately, for the blessing is in being together."*

## The greeting that ends the passage

**فَإِذَا دَخَلْتُم بُيُوتًا فَسَلِّمُوا عَلَىٰ أَنفُسِكُمْ** — "when you enter the houses, greet one another with a greeting from Allah, blessed and good." Saʿīd bin Jubayr, Al-Ḥasan Al-Baṣrī, Qatādah and Az-Zuhrī said this means greet one another with *salām*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the striking wording — "greet your own selves" — because all Muslims are a single united group.

Ibn Jurayj said: Abū Az-Zubayr said, "I heard Jābir bin ʿAbdullāh say, 'When you enter upon your family, greet them with a greeting from Allah, blessed and good.'" And Jābir said, "I do not think it is anything but obligatory." Mujāhid gave a fuller practice: when you enter the masjid, say "Peace be upon the Messenger of Allah"; when you enter upon your family, greet them with salām; and when you enter a house in which there is nobody, say *As-Salāmu ʿalaynā wa ʿalā ʿibādi-llāhi-ṣ-ṣāliḥīn* — "peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of Allah." This is what one is commanded to do, he said, and it has been narrated that the angels will return his greeting.

Ibn Kathir closes on the ayah's own last words, **لَعَلَّكُمْ تَعْقِلُونَ** — "that you may understand": having mentioned the wise rulings and reasonable, well-constructed laws contained in this surah, Allah points out to His servants that He explains His ayat to them clearly, so that they may ponder them and understand their meanings.

passages.title: True believers and the Messenger's summons
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat close Sūrah an-Nūr. They take the surah's theme of *permission* — Allah had already commanded the believers to seek permission when **entering** — and carry it into public life: how a believer behaves when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ has gathered the community, how he addresses the Prophet ﷺ, and Who is watching the whole time. What binds them together is a single idea: a believer's response to the Messenger's summons is the visible test of his faith, and Allah sees exactly how each person answers it.

## The moment behind ayah 62: the trench

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports, on the authority of Qurtubi, that this verse came down at the time of the Battle of Aḥzāb, when the Arab disbelievers and other groups joined together and suddenly attacked Madinah. After consulting the Companions, the Prophet ﷺ agreed to dig a trench as a defence — which is why the battle is also known as the Battle of the Trench (Khandaq). It was fought in Shawwāl of the fifth year of the Hijrah.

Baihaqi and Ibn Isḥāq report that the Prophet ﷺ himself took part in the digging of the trench. Against that, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing Mazharī) sets the behaviour of the hypocrites: they used to come late in the first place, and after doing a little bit of work just to show their presence, would sneak away quietly. The believers, by contrast, were putting in their best, and in case of any need or emergency would take permission from the Prophet ﷺ before leaving the work. At that point this verse was revealed.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the injunction out of this plainly: when the Prophet ﷺ calls people for a meeting in connection with jihad or any other religious matter, the demand of faith is that all should attend, and must not leave the meeting without his permission. The claim of faith is not settled by showing up; it is settled by staying, and by not walking off from a task the Messenger ﷺ has gathered you for without a word.

## "A collective matter" — and how far the ruling reaches

Ibn Kathīr places this among the matters of etiquette to which Allah has guided His believing servants: just as He commanded them to seek permission when *entering*, He also commanded them to seek permission when *leaving* — especially when they are doing something together with the Messenger ﷺ, such as the Friday, ʿĪd, or congregational prayers, or a meeting for the purpose of consultation and so on. They were not to leave him in these situations until they had asked his permission. If they did this, Ibn Kathīr says, then they were of the true believers.

A fair question arises, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises it directly: it appears from this verse that it is forbidden to get up and leave the presence of the Prophet ﷺ without seeking permission, yet there are several incidents in which Companions left his meetings when they wished and did not deem it necessary to take his permission. The answer given is that the injunction in this verse is not for ordinary meetings; it is meant for specific gatherings which the Prophet ﷺ called for some need, as was the case at the time of the Battle of the Trench.

The wording itself points to that. The verse says they were with him **ʿalā amrin jāmiʿ** — "for a collective matter." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes there are different views on what this phrase means, and says the most evident explanation is that it is used for such acts for which the Prophet ﷺ felt it necessary to collect the people, as he regarded it important to collect the people for digging the trench at the Battle of Aḥzāb (Qurtubi–Mazharī). The phrase, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, is itself pointing toward this exclusivity.

Does the ruling end with the Prophet ﷺ? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers that since this injunction is issued for a religious and Islamic need, **all the jurists agree that it is not exclusive to meetings of the Prophet ﷺ**. The same injunction applies to any Imam or ruler of the Muslims who is in control of the government, if he calls a meeting: it is obligatory to attend, and it is not lawful to leave without permission (Qurtubi–Mazharī–Bayān ul-Qurʼān).

Naturally the stress and emphasis are greatest for meetings called by the Prophet ﷺ himself, and opposing him there is open callousness. As for common meetings and gatherings not convened by a ruler, acting upon this injunction is "surely preferable and commendable" from the point of view of Islamic social etiquette: when Muslims are gathered for deliberation or action on a collective issue, one should leave the meeting only after taking permission from the presiding person.

## "Give permission to whom you will — and ask Allah's forgiveness for them"

Notice the tone of the second half of ayah 62. Allah confirms that those who ask permission are the ones who really believe in Him and His Messenger — the asking itself is treated as evidence of faith. Then, as Ibn Kathīr puts it, Allah commanded His Messenger ﷺ to give permission when someone asked for it, if he wanted to: *give permission to whom you will of them.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that if there is an emergency, permission may be sought from the Prophet ﷺ, who was advised that unless there is special need and requirement, permission may be granted on such requests.

Then comes something easy to rush past: *and ask Allah for their forgiveness.* Even the man who leaves with permission, for a real reason, is to have forgiveness sought for him. And the ayah ends with the two names that hold the whole thing: Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathīr cites here that Abū Dāwūd reported that Abū Hurayrah said, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"When any of you joins a gathering, let him say Salām, and when he wants to leave, let him say Salām. The former is not more important than the latter."* This was also recorded by at-Tirmidhī and an-Nasāʼī; at-Tirmidhī said: "It is a Ḥasan Ḥadīth." The point is exactly the passage's point: arrival and departure carry equal weight. A believer does not materialise and evaporate; he announces himself both ways.

## Ayah 63: two explanations of "the calling of the Messenger"

*"Make not the calling of the Messenger among you as your calling one of another."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the phrase can be understood in two ways: the "calling" can be the Messenger's own act, or the Messenger can be the one being called. Both yield sound meaning.

**First explanation — his call to you.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that when the Prophet ﷺ calls people, it should not be taken as the common call of an ordinary person, in which one has the choice to go or not to go. In the case of a call by the Prophet ﷺ it becomes obligatory to go to him, and leaving the meeting without his permission is unlawful. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān considers this explanation more appropriate in the context of the verse, and notes that Mazharī and Bayān ul-Qurʼān have adopted it. You can see why: it follows straight on from ayah 62, which is entirely about being gathered for a collective matter.

**Second explanation — your call to him.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this view is related by Ibn Kathīr and Qurtubi on the authority of Sayyidnā ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās. On this reading, when you call the Prophet ﷺ for some need of yours, do not call him by his name, saying "Yā Muḥammad," as you call others; this is disrespect to him. Rather, call him by an honorific form of address such as "Yā Rasūl Allāh" or "Yā Nabiyy Allāh."

Ibn Kathīr records the same from aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, reporting from Ibn ʿAbbās: "They used to say, 'O Muhammad,' or 'O Abū al-Qāsim,' but Allah forbade them to do that, as a sign of respect towards His Prophet ﷺ, and told them to say, 'O Prophet of Allah,' 'O Messenger of Allah.'" This was also the view of Mujāhid and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr. Qatādah said: "Allah commanded that His Prophet should be treated with respect and honour, and that he should be a leader." Muqātil said of the ayah: "When you address him, do not say, 'O Muhammad,' or 'O son of ʿAbdullāh'; rather honour him and say, 'O Prophet of Allah,' or, 'O Messenger of Allah.'"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets this alongside similar injunctions in Sūrah al-Ḥujurāt — for instance *"Do not raise your voices to him"* (49:2), meaning that when you talk to the Prophet ﷺ you should keep his respect in mind and not talk in a loud voice as people do when talking to each other; and *"Those who call you from behind the private apartments"* (49:4), meaning that when he is inside the house one must not call him out, but wait outside until he comes out on his own. In the final analysis, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes, it is obligatory on all Muslims to have respect and veneration for the Prophet ﷺ and to avoid all such things which are in conflict with respect and etiquette, or which may cause him inconvenience.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws one further, gentler lesson from this second explanation: as common etiquette it is incumbent upon Muslims to pay respect to their elders, and calling them by their names is disrespect — elders should always be called with titles of respect.

**A further view.** Ibn Kathīr records what he calls a second view concerning the meaning of the ayah: that it means *do not think that if he prays against you it is like when anyone else prays against you, because his prayers will be answered* — so beware lest he pray against you and you be doomed. Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded this from Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, and ʿAṭiyyah al-ʿAwfī. Ibn Kathīr closes with "and Allah knows best" — a reminder that where the early authorities differed, we hold the views as views.

## "Those who slip away under shelter"

Then the ayah turns and catches the people it was aimed at: *Allah knows those of you who slip away under shelter.*

Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān, as Ibn Kathīr reports, said: "This refers to the hypocrites who used to find it too difficult to listen to the Khutbah on Fridays, so they would hide behind some of the Companions of Muḥammad ﷺ and sneak out of the Masjid. It was not proper for a man to leave on Fridays once the Khutbah began, unless he had permission from the Prophet ﷺ. If one of them wanted to leave, he would make a gesture to the Prophet ﷺ with his finger, and the Prophet ﷺ would give permission without the man speaking. This is because if the Prophet ﷺ was giving the Khutbah and a man spoke, it would invalidate his Friday prayer." As-Suddī said: "If they were with him for a congregational prayer, they would hide behind one another so that he could not see them."

Read that against the sentence that frames it. They took cover from the Prophet's ﷺ eyes — and Allah announces that He knows every one of them. That is the sting of the passage: hypocrisy is a technique for managing what *people* can see. It has no answer at all to what Allah sees.

## The warning: going against his commandment

*"And let those beware who oppose the Messenger's commandment, lest some Fitnah should befall them or a painful torment be inflicted on them."* Ibn Kathīr reads "his commandment" broadly: this means going against the commandment of the Prophet ﷺ, which is his way, methodology and Sunnah. All words and deeds will be measured against his words and deeds; those that are in accordance with them will be accepted, and whatever does not match up will be rejected, no matter who the person is who said and did them. Ibn Kathīr cites here that it was recorded in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs and elsewhere that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"Whoever does a deed that is not in accordance with this matter of ours will have it rejected."* The warning, he says, is for those who go against the Sharīʿah of the Messenger ﷺ, in secret and in the open.

The two threatened consequences work on different levels.

**"Lest some Fitnah should befall them."** Ibn Kathīr explains this as something entering the heart: lest some disbelief, or hypocrisy, or innovation enter their hearts. The consequence of turning away from the Prophet's ﷺ way is a change in the inner person.

**"Or a painful torment be inflicted on them."** This, Ibn Kathīr says, means in this world: afflicting them with capital punishment, or by the law of prescribed punishment, or by confinement in prison, or so on. The warning is not only about the Hereafter; some of the bill is settled here.

**The parable of the fire.** Ibn Kathīr then places under this verse a ḥadīth that shows what all this warning actually is. Imām Aḥmad recorded that Abū Hurayrah said, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"The parable of me and you is as the example of a man who kindled a fire and when it illuminated all around him, moths and other creatures started falling into the fire, and he was trying to stop them but they overwhelmed him and still kept falling in. This is the parable of me and you. I am trying to restrain you and keep you away from the fire, but you overwhelm me and fall in."* This was also narrated by al-Bukhārī and Muslim.

So the command to obey him, and the warning against opposing his commandment, are not the demands of a man guarding his status. They are the grip of someone holding you back from a fire you are walking into.

## Ayah 64: the surah ends where everything ends

*"Certainly, to Allah belongs all that is in the heavens and the earth."* Ibn Kathīr says Allah tells us here that He is the Sovereign of the heavens and the earth, and that He knows the seen and the unseen — what His servants do in secret and in the open.

Then: *"Indeed, He knows your condition."* Ibn Kathīr's comment is exact: He knows it, and it is visible to Him, and not one iota is hidden from Him.

Ibn Kathīr strings together other ayat that say the same thing: that you do no deed and recite no portion of the Qurʼān but Allah is Witness of it while you are doing it, and nothing is hidden from your Lord, even the weight of a speck of dust on the earth or in the heaven (10:61); that He takes charge of every person and knows all that he has earned (13:33) — He sees all that His servants do, good and evil alike; that even when they cover themselves with their garments He knows what they conceal and what they reveal (11:5); that it is the same to Him whether any of you conceals his speech or declares it openly (13:10); that no moving creature is on earth but its provision is due from Allah, who knows its dwelling place and its deposit (11:6); and that with Him are the keys of the Unseen which none knows but He, and He knows whatever there is in the land and in the sea, and not a leaf falls but He knows it (6:59).

Then the closing clause: *and the Day when they will be brought back to Him, then He will inform them of what they did.* Ibn Kathīr explains that this is the day when all creatures will be brought back to Allah, which is the Day of Resurrection, and that He will tell them everything they did in this life, major and minor, significant and insignificant. He cites the ayah that on that Day man will be informed of what he sent forward of deeds and what he left behind (75:13), and the scene where the Book is placed and you see the criminals fearful of what is in it, saying, "Woe to us! What sort of Book is this that leaves neither a small thing nor a big thing, but has recorded it with numbers!" — and they find all that they did placed before them, and your Lord treats no one with injustice (18:49).

*And Allah is All-Knower of everything.* On that note the surah of Light ends. Ibn Kathīr closes his commentary on it with praise: "Praise be to Allah, the Lord of all that exists."

## Living it

**Answer the summons.** When the Muslims' leadership calls a meeting for a genuine collective matter, attending is obligatory, and quietly disappearing partway through is precisely the behaviour condemned in the hypocrites at the trench.

**Ask before you go.** If you must leave — and genuine need is recognised, and permission was to be granted readily on such requests — then ask. Extend this, as the jurists did, to any gathering convened for a collective issue: leave only after taking permission from the presiding person. And say Salām on the way out as you did on the way in.

**Guard how you speak of him ﷺ.** Whether the verse is explained as his call to us or ours to him, the outcome is the same: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is never handled as one of us. Honour in address, honour in tone, honour in not treating his instructions as suggestions.

**Measure yourself against his Sunnah, not your intentions.** Ibn Kathīr's rule is blunt: whatever accords with his words and deeds is accepted, whatever does not match up is rejected, no matter who the person is.

**Remember Who is watching.** The passage closes by removing the last hiding place. There is no Companion broad enough to hide behind, and no crowd dense enough to be lost in. Not one iota is hidden from Allah.
